options.C: Spacer reduces oropharyngeal deposition by 80%, eliminates coordination requirement, one actuation per inhalation, cleaned monthly with detergent then air-dried
options.D: Spacer doubles lung deposition to 40%, eliminates coordination need, multiple breaths possible from one actuation, cleaned weekly with water only then air-dried

mcqs.explanation: Option C provides accurate evidence-based information about spacer devices. Key points about spacer use: (1) Oropharyngeal deposition reduction: spacers reduce oropharyngeal deposition from 80% (pMDI alone) to approximately 15-20%, representing 80% relative reduction - critically important for ICS users as this dramatically reduces risk of oral candidiasis, dysphonia, and systemic absorption; (2) Coordination elimination: spacer acts as holding chamber allowing patient to inhale from chamber after actuation, eliminating hand-breath coordination requirement - particularly beneficial for elderly patients, those with tremor (like this patient), children, and during acute exacerbations; (3) Lung deposition: spacer increases lung deposition from 10-20% (pMDI alone) to 20-30%, not 50-60% (Option B incorrect) or 40% (Option D incorrect); (4) Actuation technique: one actuation per inhalation is correct - multiple actuations (Option B) cause propellant particles to collide and aggregate, falling to chamber bottom rather than being inhaled; patient should actuate, then take 3-5 slow tidal breaths from chamber, or one slow deep inhalation to TLC followed by 10-second breath-hold; (5) Cleaning regimen: weekly cleaning (not daily, Option A; not water only, Option D) with detergent prevents electrostatic charge buildup - new spacers have significant static charge attracting drug particles to chamber walls; washing with detergent (dishwashing liquid), rinsing, then air-drying (not towel-drying which reintroduces static) eliminates charge. Priming new spacers requires 10-20 actuations before first use. Spacer types: small volume (140-250mL) vs large volume (750mL, e.g., Volumatic, Able Spacer); both effective but large-volume better for children and severe obstruction. With spacer use, this patient's oral candidiasis should resolve due to 80% reduction in oropharyngeal ICS deposition. Additional benefits: spacer removes need for cold Freon effect tolerance, reduces cough from propellant, and maintains drug delivery even during poor inspiratory effort (National Asthma Council 2024, eTG Complete 2024-2025).
mcqs.summary: Spacer devices: reduce oropharyngeal deposition by 80% (prevents candidiasis), increase lung deposition to 20-30%, eliminate hand-breath coordination requirement. Technique: one actuation per inhalation, take 3-5 tidal breaths or one deep breath with 10-second hold. Clean weekly with detergent, air-dry (not towel). Prime new spacers with 10-20 actuations.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Australian Asthma Handbook Version 2.2 (2024)
National Asthma Council Australia - How to use a metered-dose inhaler (puffer) with spacer (2024)
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Inhaler devices and spacers (accessed January 2025)

question.scenario: An 82-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 32% predicted) and cognitive impairment from vascular dementia presents to his general practitioner with 3-day history of increasing dyspnoea and purulent sputum production. He lives in residential aged care. Nursing staff report he is unable to use his pMDI despite repeated education and spacer provision, often forgetting to inhale after actuation. Physical examination reveals respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 88% on room air, wheeze and coarse crackles throughout both lung fields. He is afebrile. His regular medications include tiotropium 18microgram daily, salbutamol 100microgram PRN (both pMDI), which nursing staff report he cannot use effectively. You diagnose acute exacerbation of COPD and commence treatment.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate method of delivering bronchodilator therapy for this patient?

options.A: Salbutamol 100microgram pMDI via large-volume spacer, four puffs four times daily with nursing staff supervision
options.B: Salbutamol 2.5mg nebuliser solution via jet nebuliser, four times daily for 5 days then review
options.C: Switch to dry powder inhaler (Turbuhaler) containing budesonide-formoterol for easier use without coordination
options.D: Ipratropium 500microgram plus salbutamol 2.5mg combined nebuliser solution, four times daily while acute, then reassess inhaler capability

mcqs.explanation: Option D (combined ipratropium-salbutamol nebuliser) is optimal for this patient with multiple indications for nebuliser therapy during acute exacerbation. Indications for nebuliser therapy include: (1) Acute severe exacerbation - this patient has acute deterioration with tachypnoea (RR 26), hypoxaemia (SpO2 88%), and increased work of breathing requiring high-dose bronchodilator delivery; (2) Cognitive impairment preventing inhaler technique - vascular dementia precludes effective use of any inhaler device requiring active participation; (3) Residential aged care setting - nursing staff can supervise nebuliser administration more reliably than complex inhaler technique; (4) Inability to use pMDI even with spacer - demonstrated treatment failure with current regimen. Nebuliser advantages: delivers high dose with minimal patient effort (only tidal breathing required), no hand-breath coordination, effective during respiratory distress, can deliver combined bronchodilators. Combined ipratropium-salbutamol (Combivent nebules) provides synergistic bronchodilation: short-acting beta-2 agonist (salbutamol) causes smooth muscle relaxation via cAMP, while short-acting muscarinic antagonist (ipratropium) blocks cholinergic bronchoconstriction - combination produces greater FEV1 improvement than either agent alone in COPD exacerbations. Nebuliser technique: use jet nebuliser (not ultrasonic, which denatures proteins), fill chamber with single unit-dose (ipratropium 500microgram + salbutamol 2.5mg in 2.5mL), connect to oxygen or air at 6-8 L/min (oxygen safe in this case as not severe CO2 retainer), nebulise until chamber empty (8-10 minutes), discard remaining solution, clean chamber daily. Option A (pMDI-spacer) already failed due to cognitive impairment. Option B (salbutamol only) suboptimal as COPD responds better to combined bronchodilators. Option C (DPI) completely inappropriate - DPIs require inspiratory flow >30 L/min and cognitive ability to coordinate breath-actuation, both absent here. After acute phase resolves, consider long-term nebuliser therapy if inhaler technique remains impossible, or discuss goals of care given advanced dementia (COPD-X Guidelines 2024, eTG Complete 2024-2025).
mcqs.summary: Nebuliser therapy indications: acute severe exacerbations, inability to use inhalers (cognitive impairment, poor technique despite education), high-dose drug delivery required. Combined ipratropium 500microgram + salbutamol 2.5mg nebuliser optimal for COPD exacerbations. Requires only tidal breathing, no coordination. Jet nebuliser at 6-8 L/min oxygen or air flow.
citations: COPD-X Australian and New Zealand Guidelines Version 2.72 (2024)
eTG Complete - Respiratory: COPD acute exacerbation - bronchodilator delivery (accessed January 2025)
Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - Nebuliser therapy (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 34-year-old woman with asthma on budesonide-formoterol 200/6microgram two puffs twice daily attends for asthma review. She reports good adherence to preventer and uses salbutamol reliever 2-3 times weekly only. No nocturnal symptoms or exercise limitation. She works as a primary school teacher. You provide her with a peak flow meter and explain how to use it. She performs three attempts with best effort: 420 L/min, 410 L/min, 425 L/min. Her predicted peak flow based on age, gender, and height (168cm) is 450 L/min. You ask her to record morning and evening peak flows daily for 2 weeks before her next appointment to assess asthma control and variability.
question.stem: What degree of peak flow variability would indicate inadequately controlled asthma requiring treatment escalation?

options.A: Average peak flow consistently >90% predicted with <10% diurnal variation
options.B: Average peak flow 80-90% predicted with 10-20% diurnal variation
options.C: Average peak flow >80% predicted with >20% diurnal variation on multiple days
options.D: Average peak flow <80% predicted regardless of variability pattern

mcqs.explanation: Option C correctly identifies excessive peak flow variability (>20%) as indicator of inadequate asthma control requiring treatment review, even when absolute values appear reasonable. Peak flow monitoring principles: (1) Diurnal variation calculation: [(best - worst) / best] × 100% - normally <10% in well-controlled asthma; >20% indicates airway hyperresponsiveness and labile bronchoconstriction characteristic of poorly controlled asthma; (2) Personal best: patient's highest peak flow reading when well, not predicted value - predicted values based on age, sex, height are reference only (this patient's predicted 450 L/min, current best 425 L/min = 94% predicted, acceptable); (3) Traffic light zones: Green >80% personal best (well controlled), Yellow 60-80% (caution, may need reliever), Red <60% (medical help needed); (4) Pattern recognition: progressive decline over days suggests deteriorating control, diurnal variation >20% indicates instability. This patient's current peak flows (410-425 L/min) are 94% of predicted and likely represent her current personal best, appearing satisfactory. However, if 2-week monitoring reveals >20% diurnal variation on multiple days (e.g., morning 340 L/min, evening 425 L/min = 20% variation), this indicates significant airway lability despite apparently good absolute values and symptom control. Excessive variability predicts increased exacerbation risk, nocturnal awakening, and suboptimal long-term outcomes. Clinical significance: >20% variability suggests insufficient anti-inflammatory control despite current ICS dose. Management escalation options: (1) Increase ICS dose (budesonide-formoterol 400/12 microgram); (2) Add leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast 10mg nocte); (3) Check adherence and inhaler technique (most common cause of apparent treatment failure); (4) Identify and address triggers (occupational, allergens). Option A (<10% variation) indicates excellent control. Option B (10-20% variation with 80-90% predicted) suggests reasonable but suboptimal control, warrants close monitoring but not necessarily immediate escalation. Option D focuses only on absolute values without considering variability - patient could have 78% predicted with <10% variation (acceptable) or 85% predicted with >25% variation (unacceptable). Peak flow variability is independent predictor of asthma outcomes, sometimes more sensitive than absolute values for detecting inadequate control (National Asthma Council Asthma Handbook 2024, eTG Complete 2024-2025).
mcqs.summary: Peak flow monitoring: >20% diurnal variation indicates inadequate asthma control requiring treatment review, even if absolute values >80% predicted. Calculate: [(best-worst)/best] × 100%. Normal <10% variation. Personal best more important than predicted values. Excessive variability predicts exacerbations and warrants ICS escalation or additional controller.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Australian Asthma Handbook Version 2.2 (2024)
National Asthma Council Australia - Peak flow monitoring in asthma (2024)
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma assessment and monitoring (accessed January 2025)

question.scenario: A 58-year-old man with 30-pack-year smoking history (ceased 2 years ago) presents with 18-month history of progressive exertional dyspnoea and occasional dry cough. Denies wheeze, nocturnal symptoms, or childhood respiratory problems. Physical examination reveals reduced breath sounds bilaterally with quiet expiratory wheeze. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation without focal consolidation. Spirometry performed: FVC 3.8L (90% predicted), FEV1 2.1L (61% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.55. Post-bronchodilator spirometry after 400microgram salbutamol shows FEV1 2.25L (65% predicted), FVC 3.9L (92% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.58. Improvement in FEV1 is 150mL (7% increase from baseline).
question.stem: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this spirometry result?

options.A: Normal spirometry excluding significant respiratory disease
options.B: COPD with irreversible airflow obstruction, GOLD Grade 2 (moderate)
options.C: Asthma-COPD overlap syndrome due to significant bronchodilator response
options.D: Restrictive lung disease requiring lung volume measurement with body plethysmography

mcqs.explanation: Option B correctly identifies this as COPD with irreversible obstruction, GOLD Grade 2 severity. Key spirometric interpretations: (1) Obstructive pattern confirmed: FEV1/FVC ratio 0.55 (post-bronchodilator 0.58) - both <0.70 threshold diagnostic for obstructive disease; this ratio is more sensitive and specific than FEV1 alone for diagnosing airflow obstruction; (2) FEV1 reduction: 61% predicted (post-bronchodilator 65%) indicates moderate severity; preserved FVC (90% predicted) rules out restrictive pattern; (3) GOLD classification: uses post-bronchodilator FEV1: GOLD 1 (mild) ≥80% predicted, GOLD 2 (moderate) 50-79% predicted, GOLD 3 (severe) 30-49% predicted, GOLD 4 (very severe) <30% predicted - this patient has FEV1 65% = GOLD 2; (4) Bronchodilator response: 150mL absolute improvement but only 7% relative increase - does NOT meet criteria for significant reversibility (requires ≥12% AND ≥200mL); patients with COPD may show some bronchodilator response due to reversible smooth muscle component, but response <12% AND/OR <200mL indicates predominantly irreversible (structural) obstruction from emphysema/airway remodeling; (5) Clinical context: 30-pack-year smoking history, progressive symptoms, no features of asthma (no variability, nocturnal symptoms, wheeze), consistent with smoking-related COPD. Post-bronchodilator spirometry is mandatory for COPD diagnosis as it eliminates reversible bronchoconstriction and standardises measurement. Option A incorrect - clearly abnormal with FEV1/FVC <0.70 and reduced FEV1. Option C incorrect - ACOS requires significant reversibility (≥12% AND ≥200mL absolute) plus other asthma features (eosinophilia, variable symptoms, atopy); this patient has 150mL (insufficient) and 7% (insufficient). Option D incorrect - restrictive disease shows proportional reduction in FEV1 and FVC with preserved ratio (>0.70); this patient has reduced ratio and preserved FVC, classic for obstruction. Management: smoking cessation most important intervention (slows FEV1 decline from 60mL/year to 30mL/year), commence LAMA (tiotropium) or LABA-LAMA combination, pneumococcal and influenza vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation referral (COPD-X Guidelines 2024, eTG Complete 2024-2025).
mcqs.summary: COPD diagnosis: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms obstruction. GOLD severity: Grade 1 FEV1 ≥80%, Grade 2 50-79%, Grade 3 30-49%, Grade 4 <30% predicted. Significant reversibility: ≥12% AND ≥200mL increase (if met, suggests ACOS). Post-bronchodilator values essential for diagnosis and classification.
citations: COPD-X Australian and New Zealand Guidelines Version 2.72 (2024)
eTG Complete - Respiratory: COPD diagnosis and spirometry interpretation (accessed January 2025)
Lung Foundation Australia - Spirometry Quality Assurance Manual (2024)

question.scenario: A 42-year-old woman presents with 6-month history of variable dyspnoea and wheeze, worse at night and with exercise. She reports needing salbutamol reliever 4-5 days per week. No smoking history. Childhood eczema but no previous asthma diagnosis. Physical examination normal with no wheeze audible today. Baseline spirometry performed: FVC 3.6L (95% predicted), FEV1 2.6L (78% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.72. You arrange bronchodilator response testing. Patient administered 400microgram salbutamol (four puffs of 100microgram via spacer). Spirometry repeated after 15 minutes: FVC 3.7L (97% predicted), FEV1 3.1L (93% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.84. Absolute FEV1 improvement 500mL, relative improvement 19%.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this bronchodilator response?

options.A: Normal spirometry and bronchodilator response, excludes asthma diagnosis
options.B: Significant bronchodilator reversibility supporting asthma diagnosis
options.C: Borderline reversibility requiring further testing with inhaled corticosteroid trial
options.D: Fixed airflow obstruction indicating COPD despite never smoking

mcqs.explanation: Option B correctly identifies significant bronchodilator reversibility strongly supporting asthma diagnosis. Bronchodilator response testing interpretation: (1) Criteria for significant reversibility: increase in FEV1 ≥12% (relative) AND ≥200mL (absolute) from baseline - both criteria must be met; this patient demonstrates 500mL (absolute, well exceeds 200mL threshold) and 19% (relative, exceeds 12% threshold), indicating marked reversibility characteristic of asthma; (2) Baseline FEV1/FVC ratio 0.72 - this is actually above the 0.70 threshold for obstruction, suggesting airflow limitation was present but mild (FEV1 78% predicted indicates mild reduction); alternatively, patient may have normal spirometry at time of testing (asthma shows temporal variability) with reversibility test 'unmasking' potential for airway narrowing; (3) Post-bronchodilator normalisation: FEV1 improved from 78% to 93% predicted, FEV1/FVC from 0.72 to 0.84 - this normalisation after bronchodilator strongly suggests reversible disease (asthma) rather than fixed obstruction (COPD); (4) Clinical context: variable symptoms, nocturnal and exercise-triggered, childhood atopy (eczema), no smoking history, young age - all favour asthma over COPD. Magnitude of response (500mL, 19%) is substantial, often seen in untreated asthma with significant bronchospasm at baseline. Bronchodilator testing protocol: cease SABA ≥6 hours before test, LABA ≥12 hours, LAMA ≥24 hours (ensure testing true baseline); perform baseline spirometry (three attempts, reproducible within 150mL); administer 400microgram salbutamol via spacer; wait 10-15 minutes for peak effect; repeat spirometry. Some patients with asthma have normal baseline spirometry (particularly if tested when asymptomatic) but demonstrate hyperresponsiveness on bronchial provocation testing (methacholine, exercise, mannitol). Option A incorrect - significant reversibility documented. Option C incorrect - clear-cut reversibility present, ICS trial unnecessary for diagnosis (though appropriate treatment). Option D incorrect - no obstruction present (ratio >0.70), reversibility rules out fixed obstruction. Diagnosis: asthma confirmed by significant reversibility. Commence ICS-containing therapy (budesonide-formoterol 200/6 microgram twice daily or fluticasone propionate 125microgram twice daily), review in 4-6 weeks, aim for complete symptom control (National Asthma Council 2024, eTG Complete 2024-2025).
mcqs.summary: Significant bronchodilator reversibility: FEV1 increase ≥12% AND ≥200mL (both criteria required). This patient shows 500mL (absolute) and 19% (relative) improvement, strongly supporting asthma diagnosis. Post-bronchodilator normalisation characteristic of reversible airway disease. Commence ICS therapy. Absence of reversibility doesn't exclude asthma - may need bronchial provocation testing.

Lung Foundation Australia - Spirometry Quality Assurance Manual (2024)

question.scenario: A 28-year-old woman presents to respiratory clinic with difficult-to-control asthma despite fluticasone propionate 250microgram twice daily and salbutamol as required. She reports persistent wheeze, dyspnoea 3-4 days weekly, and nocturnal waking twice weekly. Childhood asthma diagnosis, multiple pets at home (two cats, one dog), works as hairdresser. Non-smoker. Spirometry shows FEV1 68% predicted with reversibility to 82% predicted after bronchodilator (400microgram salbutamol). Blood eosinophil count 420 cells/microlitre. Her respiratory physician requests fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) measurement to guide treatment escalation. FeNO result: 52 parts per billion (ppb).
question.stem: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this FeNO result in guiding asthma management?

options.A: FeNO <25ppb excludes eosinophilic asthma; consider non-eosinophilic phenotype treatment
options.B: FeNO 25-40ppb suggests possible eosinophilic inflammation; repeat after ICS optimisation
options.C: FeNO >40ppb indicates eosinophilic airway inflammation; likely ICS-responsive, consider dose escalation or check adherence
options.D: FeNO >50ppb diagnostic for asthma regardless of spirometry; commence biologics immediately

mcqs.explanation: Option C correctly interprets elevated FeNO (52ppb, >40ppb threshold) as indicating eosinophilic (Type 2) airway inflammation, with important treatment implications. FeNO (Fractional exhaled Nitric Oxide) interpretation: (1) Normal values: <25ppb in adults makes eosinophilic asthma unlikely; <20ppb in children; (2) Intermediate: 25-40ppb suggests possible eosinophilic inflammation, interpret with clinical context; (3) Elevated: >40ppb adults (>35ppb children) indicates eosinophilic inflammation with high probability of ICS responsiveness. FeNO is produced by airway epithelial cells in response to Type 2 inflammation driven by interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 (eosinophilic pathway). This patient's FeNO 52ppb, combined with elevated blood eosinophils (420 cells/microlitre, threshold >150-300 depending on context), strongly confirms eosinophilic phenotype. Clinical implications: (1) ICS responsiveness predicted: elevated FeNO indicates patients likely to respond to ICS therapy or ICS dose increase; (2) Adherence assessment: persistent elevation despite ICS suggests either non-adherence (check prescription refills, inhaler technique) or insufficient dose; (3) Treatment escalation: if adherent with good technique, increase ICS dose (fluticasone 500microgram twice daily) or add leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast), or consider ICS-LABA combination; (4) Biologics consideration: persistent uncontrolled asthma with FeNO >40ppb and eosinophils >300 may qualify for biologics (anti-IL-5, anti-IgE, anti-IL-4/13 receptor) after optimising conventional therapy and confirming adherence. FeNO declines with effective ICS therapy (useful monitoring tool). Factors increasing FeNO: atopy, allergic rhinitis, eczema, viral infections, non-adherence to ICS. Factors decreasing FeNO: smoking (this patient non-smoker), recent ICS use. This patient likely has occupational triggers (hairdresser - exposure to ammonia, bleach, aerosols) and allergen exposure (multiple pets) contributing to poor control. Option A incorrect - FeNO is elevated not low. Option B incorrect - FeNO clearly elevated >40ppb, not intermediate range. Option D incorrect - FeNO doesn't diagnose asthma alone (requires clinical symptoms + objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction); biologics not immediate next step before optimising ICS adherence/dose and addressing triggers. Management: (1) Verify ICS adherence and technique; (2) Increase ICS or add LABA; (3) Address allergen exposure (pets) and occupational triggers; (4) Consider montelukast; (5) If uncontrolled after 3-6 months optimal therapy, consider biologics referral (National Asthma Council 2024, eTG Complete 2024-2025).
mcqs.summary: FeNO interpretation: <25ppb unlikely eosinophilic asthma, 25-40ppb intermediate (possible eosinophilic), >40ppb eosinophilic inflammation (ICS-responsive). Elevated FeNO (>40ppb) + eosinophils >300 predicts ICS responsiveness and potential biologics benefit. Use FeNO to guide ICS dose escalation and monitor adherence. Factors affecting: atopy increases, smoking decreases.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Australian Asthma Handbook Version 2.2 (2024)
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - FeNO testing (accessed January 2025)
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners - FeNO in asthma management (2024)

question.scenario: A 38-year-old woman with severe persistent allergic asthma attends respiratory clinic for treatment review. Despite maximal conventional therapy (fluticasone propionate 500microgram + salmeterol 50microgram twice daily, montelukast 10mg nocte, excellent adherence verified), she experiences 6-8 exacerbations yearly requiring oral prednisolone, with two hospitalisations in past 12 months. Current Asthma Control Test score 14/25 (poorly controlled). Skin prick testing: positive to house dust mite, cat dander, grass pollens (≥3mm wheal). Serum total IgE: 580 IU/mL. Blood eosinophil count: 280 cells/microlitre. FEV1 62% predicted. Her respiratory physician discusses biologics therapy and refers to immunology for consideration of targeted treatment.
question.stem: Which biologic agent is most appropriate as first-line therapy for this patient?

options.A: Mepolizumab (anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody) 100mg subcutaneously monthly
options.B: Omalizumab (anti-IgE monoclonal antibody) dosed by weight and IgE level, subcutaneously 2-4 weekly
options.C: Benralizumab (anti-IL-5 receptor alpha monoclonal antibody) 30mg subcutaneously
options.D: Dupilumab (anti-IL-4 receptor alpha monoclonal antibody) 200mg subcutaneously 2-weekly

mcqs.explanation: Option B (omalizumab) is most appropriate first-line biologic for this patient with severe allergic asthma meeting specific criteria. Biologics for severe asthma target Type 2 (eosinophilic) inflammation pathways. Patient selection based on phenotype: (1) ALLERGIC ASTHMA phenotype: elevated IgE, positive specific IgE or skin prick tests to perennial allergens, age ≥6 years → Omalizumab (anti-IgE); (2) EOSINOPHILIC ASTHMA phenotype: elevated eosinophils without prominent allergic features → Anti-IL-5 pathway (mepolizumab, benralizumab, reslizumab). This patient demonstrates allergic phenotype: positive skin prick tests to multiple perennial allergens (house dust mite, cat dander - year-round exposure), elevated total IgE (580 IU/mL, within omalizumab dosing range 30-1500 IU/mL), severe uncontrolled asthma despite maximal therapy. Omalizumab mechanism: binds free IgE, preventing IgE attachment to mast cells and basophils, reducing allergic cascade. Dosing: calculated by body weight (kg) and baseline IgE level (IU/mL) using manufacturer's dosing table, typically 150-375mg subcutaneously every 2-4 weeks. Efficacy: reduces exacerbations by 40-50%, improves asthma control and quality of life, allows oral corticosteroid reduction. PBS listing (Australia): requires (1) Severe persistent allergic asthma confirmed by respiratory physician or immunologist; (2) Age ≥6 years; (3) IgE 30-1500 IU/mL; (4) Positive skin prick or specific IgE to perennial allergen; (5) ≥4 documented severe exacerbations in previous 12 months OR continuous/frequent oral corticosteroids; (6) Documented trial of high-dose ICS-LABA, LTRA, excellent adherence. Patient requires specialist initiation, first three doses given in clinical setting (anaphylaxis risk <0.2%), then may self-administer. Response assessment at 16 weeks - continue if improved (≥50% exacerbation reduction or significant symptom improvement). Option A (mepolizumab): anti-IL-5, approved for eosinophilic asthma (eosinophils ≥150 in past 12 months OR ≥300 at baseline), PBS requires eosinophil threshold - this patient has eosinophils 280, borderline, but allergic phenotype makes omalizumab preferred. Option C (benralizumab): anti-IL-5 receptor alpha, for eosinophilic asthma, PBS requires eosinophils ≥300, more potent eosinophil depletion than mepolizumab - not first-line here. Option D (dupilumab): anti-IL-4 receptor alpha (blocks IL-4 and IL-13), effective for eosinophilic and allergic asthma, but currently PBS-listed primarily for atopic dermatitis with asthma, not first-line for asthma alone in Australia. Omalizumab is most appropriate given clear allergic phenotype with IgE in range (National Asthma Council 2024, PBS Schedule 2025).
mcqs.summary: Omalizumab (anti-IgE) first-line biologic for severe allergic asthma: requires positive skin prick/specific IgE to perennial allergens, IgE 30-1500 IU/mL, ≥4 exacerbations yearly, maximal conventional therapy failed. Dosed by weight and IgE level. PBS requires specialist initiation. Mepolizumab/benralizumab for eosinophilic phenotype (eosinophils ≥150-300). Assess response at 16 weeks.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Australian Asthma Handbook Version 2.2 (2024)
Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) - Omalizumab (Xolair) restrictions (accessed January 2025)
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Severe asthma - biologic therapies (accessed January 2025)

question.scenario: A 52-year-old man with severe allergic asthma has been on omalizumab (Xolair) 300mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks for the past 5 months. Pre-treatment, he experienced 8-10 exacerbations yearly requiring oral corticosteroids and three hospital admissions. His baseline IgE was 420 IU/mL, weight 78kg, with positive skin prick tests to house dust mite, Alternaria, and cat dander. Pre-omalizumab FEV1 was 58% predicted, Asthma Control Test 11/25. Current medications: fluticasone propionate 500microgram + salmeterol 50microgram twice daily, montelukast 10mg nocte, omalizumab. He returns for 6-month review. Since commencing omalizumab, he has had one mild exacerbation managed with increased salbutamol only, no hospitalisations. Current FEV1 69% predicted, ACT score 21/25. He reports significant improvement in quality of life but is concerned about long-term injection requirements and costs. Omalizumab costs $1,200 per month under PBS with patient contribution.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate management recommendation regarding omalizumab continuation?

options.A: Discontinue omalizumab after 6 months as maximum benefit achieved; maintain ICS-LABA and monitor
options.B: Continue omalizumab with plan for indefinite long-term treatment while severe asthma persists
options.C: Attempt trial of omalizumab cessation with close monitoring; restart if exacerbations recur within 3 months
options.D: Switch to mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) as maintenance therapy is more cost-effective with monthly dosing

mcqs.explanation: Option B (continue omalizumab long-term) is correct management for this patient demonstrating excellent response. Omalizumab continuation criteria and monitoring: (1) Response assessment: performed at 16 weeks initially, then 6-monthly - response defined as ≥50% reduction in clinically significant exacerbations OR significant improvement in asthma control (ACT increase ≥3 points) OR improvement in lung function OR reduction in oral corticosteroid requirement; this patient demonstrates marked response: exacerbations reduced from 8-10/year to one mild episode in 6 months (>90% reduction), ACT improved from 11 to 21 (10-point improvement, clinically significant as ≥3 points), FEV1 improved from 58% to 69% predicted (11% improvement), zero hospitalisations; (2) Duration of therapy: omalizumab requires ongoing treatment to maintain benefit - asthma control deteriorates within weeks to months of cessation in most patients as IgE-mediated inflammation recurs; biologics are disease-controlling not disease-modifying; (3) PBS continuation criteria (Australia): patients demonstrating adequate response at 16 weeks qualify for continuing PBS authority, requiring respiratory physician or immunologist review every 6-12 months with documentation of ongoing severe asthma and continued benefit; (4) Safety profile: omalizumab well-tolerated long-term (safety data >10 years), main adverse effects: injection site reactions (45%), headache (15%), rare anaphylaxis (<0.2%, mainly first three doses); (5) Cost-effectiveness: while expensive ($1,200/month PBS cost, patient copayment ~$42/script or $7.70 concession), cost-effectiveness analyses show omalizumab reduces total healthcare costs by preventing exacerbations, hospitalisations, emergency presentations, and oral corticosteroid complications (osteoporosis, diabetes, adrenal suppression). For patients with severe asthma requiring frequent exacerbations or continuous oral corticosteroids, preventing even 1-2 hospitalisations yearly offsets medication cost. This patient's response is excellent - continuing therapy essential to maintain benefit. Option A (discontinue at 6 months) inappropriate - maximum benefit may take 12+ months to achieve, early cessation results in relapse. Studies show continued benefit with prolonged therapy (some patients treated >10 years successfully). Option C (trial cessation) not recommended when patient responding well - unnecessary risk of severe exacerbation, loss of asthma control, possible hospitalisation. Cessation might be considered if: minimal or no response after 6-12 months adequate trial, or asthma control dramatically improved allowing step-down of all other therapies (rare). Option D (switch to mepolizumab) illogical - patient responding excellently to omalizumab, switching risks losing control. Mepolizumab targets different pathway (IL-5, eosinophilic phenotype) - this patient has allergic phenotype. Never switch biologics in responding patients unless adverse effects occur. Continue omalizumab indefinitely with 6-monthly reviews (National Asthma Council 2024, PBS guidelines 2025, eTG Complete 2024-2025).
mcqs.summary: Omalizumab requires ongoing long-term treatment (often years) to maintain benefit in severe allergic asthma. Response assessed at 16 weeks then 6-monthly: ≥50% exacerbation reduction or significant ACT improvement defines response. PBS continuation requires documented ongoing severe asthma and continued benefit. Well-tolerated long-term. Cessation leads to relapse within weeks-months. Cost-effective by preventing hospitalisations and oral corticosteroid complications.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Australian Asthma Handbook Version 2.2 (2024)
Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) - Omalizumab continuing treatment criteria (accessed January 2025)

question.scenario: A 45-year-old office worker presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, productive cough with purulent sputum, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination, temperature is 38.7°C, heart rate 102 bpm, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Chest examination reveals bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right lower zone. Chest X-ray demonstrates right lower lobe consolidation.
question.stem: According to Australian guidelines for community-acquired pneumonia diagnosis, which additional investigation is MOST important to guide initial antibiotic therapy?

options.A: Blood cultures and sputum microscopy/culture before commencing antibiotics
options.B: CT chest with contrast to delineate extent of consolidation
options.C: Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage for definitive pathogen identification
options.D: Serology for atypical organisms including Mycoplasma and Legionella

mcqs.explanation: According to eTG Complete and Australian guidelines, blood cultures and sputum microscopy/culture should be obtained BEFORE commencing antibiotic therapy in hospitalised patients with community-acquired pneumonia. This is particularly important for patients requiring admission, as it allows for pathogen identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, which can guide targeted therapy if the patient fails to respond to empirical treatment or if there are concerns about resistant organisms. Sputum samples should be obtained from patients with a productive cough before antibiotics are administered, as antibiotic therapy rapidly reduces the yield of cultures. Blood cultures are positive in approximately 10-20% of hospitalised CAP patients and can identify the causative organism and guide de-escalation of therapy. While empirical antibiotic therapy should not be delayed for investigation results, obtaining cultures before antibiotics maximises diagnostic yield. CT chest (option B) is not routinely required for CAP diagnosis unless there are complications or diagnostic uncertainty. Bronchoscopy (option C) is reserved for patients not responding to appropriate therapy or when there is suspicion of alternative diagnoses. Acute serology (option D) has limited utility as it does not influence initial management; serological diagnosis requires convalescent samples and is mainly of epidemiological interest. The key principle is that while investigations should be performed promptly, they should not delay appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy, which should commence within 4 hours of hospital presentation for severe CAP according to Australian quality standards.
mcqs.summary: Blood cultures and sputum microscopy/culture before antibiotics are essential in hospitalised CAP patients per eTG guidelines. These investigations maximise pathogen identification and allow antimicrobial susceptibility testing to guide therapy. Empirical antibiotics should not be delayed but cultures must be obtained first to maintain diagnostic yield.
citations: eTG Complete - Respiratory: Community-acquired pneumonia (2024-2025)
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pneumonia, community-acquired (2024)
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care - Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard (2024)

question.scenario: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, cough productive of green sputum, and shortness of breath. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. On examination, he appears mildly confused (AMTS 8/10), temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 108 bpm, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Chest examination reveals right-sided crackles and bronchial breathing. Blood tests show: urea 9.2 mmol/L, creatinine 118 μmol/L. Chest X-ray confirms right middle lobe pneumonia.
question.stem: What is this patient's CURB-65 score and the most appropriate management setting according to Australian guidelines?

options.A: CURB-65 score 2; suitable for outpatient management with oral antibiotics
options.B: CURB-65 score 3; requires hospital admission with consideration for intensive care assessment
options.C: CURB-65 score 4; requires immediate ICU admission
options.D: CURB-65 score 1; suitable for hospital-in-the-home program with oral antibiotics

mcqs.explanation: The CURB-65 score is a validated clinical prediction tool used in Australia to assess pneumonia severity and guide the decision regarding site of care. The five criteria are: Confusion (AMTS ≤8 or new disorientation), Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30 breaths/min, Blood pressure (systolic <90 mmHg or diastolic ≤60 mmHg), and age ≥65 years. Each criterion scores 1 point. This patient scores 4 points: (1) Confusion present (AMTS 8/10), (2) Urea elevated at 9.2 mmol/L (>7 mmol/L threshold), (3) Respiratory rate 32 breaths/min (≥30 threshold), and (4) Age 72 years (≥65 threshold). The blood pressure 118/72 mmHg does not meet the hypotension criterion. According to eTG Complete and Australian guidelines: CURB-65 score 0-1 suggests low risk suitable for outpatient management; score 2 indicates intermediate risk requiring hospital admission; score 3-5 indicates high risk with significantly increased mortality requiring hospital admission and consideration for intensive care unit assessment. With a score of 4, this patient has severe CAP with an estimated 30-day mortality risk of approximately 15-40% depending on additional factors. He requires urgent hospital admission, intravenous antibiotic therapy, and assessment by the intensive care team. The score is incorrectly calculated in option C (score 4 is correct, not requiring immediate ICU admission but ICU assessment). Options A and D underestimate severity. Australian guidelines recommend considering ICU admission for CURB-65 ≥3, particularly with additional adverse features such as hypoxaemia, multilobar involvement, or comorbidities like diabetes.
mcqs.summary: CURB-65 assesses CAP severity using five criteria (Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30, Blood pressure <90/60, age ≥65). This patient scores 4 points (confusion, urea 9.2, RR 32, age 72). Score 3-5 indicates high risk requiring hospital admission and ICU consideration per Australian guidelines, with mortality risk 15-40%.
citations: eTG Complete - Respiratory: Community-acquired pneumonia - Assessment of severity (2024-2025)
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pneumonia, community-acquired - Severity assessment (2024)
Lim WS et al. Thorax 2003;58:377-382 (CURB-65 validation study)

question.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with community-acquired pneumonia has been assessed using both CURB-65 and the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI). She has fever, cough, and dyspnoea. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and congestive cardiac failure. Vital signs: temperature 38.5°C, heart rate 95 bpm, blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Blood results show pH 7.38, sodium 136 mmol/L, glucose 6.2 mmol/L, haematocrit 38%, urea 6.8 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation without pleural effusion. The medical team is comparing severity scoring systems to guide management.
question.stem: Compared to CURB-65, what is the PRIMARY advantage of the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) in risk stratification for community-acquired pneumonia?

options.A: PSI is simpler to calculate at the bedside without requiring laboratory investigations
options.B: PSI incorporates more clinical and laboratory variables providing more granular risk stratification into five risk classes
options.C: PSI has been specifically validated in Australian populations whereas CURB-65 was validated only in European populations
options.D: PSI better identifies patients suitable for intensive care admission compared to CURB-65

mcqs.explanation: The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI), also known as the PORT score (Pneumonia Outcomes Research Team), is a more complex risk stratification tool that incorporates 20 variables including demographic factors (age, sex, nursing home residence), comorbidities (neoplastic disease, liver disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, renal disease), physical examination findings (altered mental status, respiratory rate ≥30, systolic BP <90, temperature <35°C or ≥40°C, pulse ≥125), and laboratory/radiographic findings (pH <7.35, urea ≥11 mmol/L, sodium <130 mmol/L, glucose ≥14 mmol/L, haematocrit <30%, PaO2 <60 mmHg, pleural effusion). These variables generate a point score that classifies patients into five risk classes (I-V) with increasing 30-day mortality risk: Class I (0.1%), Class II (0.6%), Class III (0.9-2.8%), Class IV (8.2-9.3%), and Class V (27-31%). The primary advantage of PSI over CURB-65 is this more granular risk stratification, particularly its ability to identify very low-risk patients (Classes I-II) who may be suitable for outpatient management. However, PSI's complexity (option A is incorrect) limits bedside utility compared to CURB-65's simplicity. Both tools have been validated internationally including in Australian settings (option C is incorrect). While PSI provides detailed risk stratification, CURB-65 is actually considered superior for identifying patients requiring ICU admission (option D is incorrect), with CURB-65 ≥3 or individual criteria like hypotension being strong ICU predictors. In Australian practice, eTG Complete acknowledges both tools but favours CURB-65 for its simplicity and practicality, while noting PSI's value in research settings and for identifying very low-risk patients who can be safely managed as outpatients.
mcqs.summary: PSI (Pneumonia Severity Index) incorporates 20 clinical and laboratory variables to stratify CAP patients into five risk classes (I-V) with granular mortality prediction (0.1-31%). While more complex than CURB-65, PSI excels at identifying very low-risk patients suitable for outpatient care. Australian guidelines favour CURB-65 for simplicity but acknowledge PSI's research value.
citations: eTG Complete - Respiratory: Community-acquired pneumonia - Assessment of severity (2024-2025)
Fine MJ et al. N Engl J Med 1997;336:243-250 (PSI/PORT validation study)
Chalmers JD et al. Clin Infect Dis 2010;50:1331-1336 (CURB-65 vs PSI comparison)

question.scenario: A 38-year-old previously healthy woman presents to her general practitioner with a 2-day history of fever, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right-sided chest pain worse on deep inspiration. She has no drug allergies and is not pregnant. On examination, temperature is 38.2°C, heart rate 88 bpm, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Chest examination reveals reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the right mid-zone. The GP diagnoses community-acquired pneumonia and assesses severity as mild (CURB-65 score 0).
question.stem: According to current Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate first-line antibiotic regimen for outpatient management of this patient?

options.A: Amoxycillin 500 mg three times daily orally for 5 days
options.B: Amoxycillin 1 g three times daily orally for 5 days OR doxycycline 100 mg twice daily orally for 5 days
options.C: Amoxycillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily orally plus azithromycin 500 mg daily orally for 5 days
options.D: Roxithromycin 300 mg once daily orally for 7 days

mcqs.explanation: According to eTG Complete and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic (2024), the first-line treatment for mild community-acquired pneumonia in previously healthy adults suitable for outpatient management is either amoxycillin 1 g orally three times daily for 5 days OR doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days. Note the Australian spelling 'amoxycillin' (with 'y') which differs from the American 'amoxicillin'. The higher dose of amoxycillin (1 g three times daily, not 500 mg as in option A) is recommended to ensure adequate coverage of Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common causative organism, including strains with reduced penicillin susceptibility. Doxycycline provides an alternative for patients with penicillin allergy or intolerance, and also covers atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydophila pneumoniae. The guidelines emphasise that monotherapy is appropriate for mild CAP in previously healthy individuals, as combination therapy has not been shown to improve outcomes in this low-risk group and increases costs and potential adverse effects. Option C (amoxycillin-clavulanate plus azithromycin) represents over-treatment for uncomplicated mild CAP; combination therapy is reserved for moderate-severity outpatient CAP or specific situations such as suspected aspiration. Option D (roxithromycin monotherapy) could be considered in penicillin allergy but is not listed as first-line in current guidelines. The recommended duration is 5 days for uncomplicated cases, which is shorter than historically used regimens and supported by recent evidence showing equivalent outcomes with reduced antibiotic exposure. Treatment duration should be guided by clinical response, with extension to 7 days if slow improvement. This approach aligns with Australian antimicrobial stewardship principles of using narrow-spectrum, targeted therapy for the shortest effective duration.
mcqs.summary: First-line treatment for mild CAP (CURB-65 score 0) in previously healthy adults is amoxycillin 1 g three times daily orally OR doxycycline 100 mg twice daily orally for 5 days per eTG 2024-2025. Monotherapy is appropriate for mild cases; combination therapy is unnecessary and increases adverse effects. Duration is 5 days for uncomplicated cases, supporting antimicrobial stewardship.
citations: eTG Complete - Respiratory: Community-acquired pneumonia - Mild severity (2024-2025)
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pneumonia, community-acquired - Outpatient management (2024)
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care - Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard (2024)

question.scenario: A 42-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia is being treated with oral amoxycillin 1 g three times daily. He has completed 3 days of therapy and returns to his GP for review. He reports that his fever has resolved, cough is improving with less purulent sputum production, and chest pain has decreased. On examination, temperature is 37.1°C, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and chest examination shows resolving signs with scattered crackles in the right lower zone. He asks about the duration of antibiotic therapy and when he might expect complete resolution of symptoms.
question.stem: According to Australian guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate advice regarding amoxycillin therapy duration and expected clinical resolution for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia?

options.A: Continue amoxycillin for a total of 10-14 days to prevent relapse; complete symptom resolution expected within 7 days
options.B: Complete a 5-day course of amoxycillin; clinical improvement should continue but complete radiological resolution may take 4-6 weeks
options.C: Stop amoxycillin now as fever has resolved; residual symptoms require no further antibiotic therapy
options.D: Continue amoxycillin for 7 days total and order repeat chest X-ray in 48 hours to confirm radiological improvement before stopping antibiotics

mcqs.explanation: According to eTG Complete and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic (2024), the recommended duration for oral amoxycillin in uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia is 5 days, provided there is satisfactory clinical response. This patient demonstrates appropriate clinical improvement with fever resolution, reduced cough, decreased sputum production, and improved chest pain, indicating treatment success. Recent evidence, including the CAP-IT trial and meta-analyses, supports shorter antibiotic courses (5 days) as non-inferior to traditional longer courses (7-10 days) for uncomplicated CAP in terms of clinical cure and mortality, while reducing antibiotic exposure and potential adverse effects. This aligns with Australian antimicrobial stewardship principles. Patients should be counselled that while clinical symptoms improve within 3-7 days, complete symptom resolution may take several weeks, and radiological resolution (clearing of chest X-ray infiltrates) typically takes 4-6 weeks or longer, particularly in older patients or those with multilobar pneumonia. The persistence of radiological changes does not indicate treatment failure if clinical improvement is occurring. Option A (10-14 days) represents outdated practice; prolonged therapy is only indicated for complicated pneumonia (empyema, lung abscess, bacteraemia with slow response) or specific pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus. Option C is incorrect as stopping at day 3 is premature despite fever resolution; the 5-day course should be completed. Option D is unnecessary; routine follow-up chest X-ray is not required in uncomplicated CAP with satisfactory clinical response. Follow-up imaging is indicated only if there is lack of clinical improvement by 6 weeks, or concern for underlying malignancy (particularly in smokers >50 years), to ensure complete radiological resolution. The key principle is treating based on clinical response rather than radiological clearance.
mcqs.summary: Uncomplicated CAP should be treated with amoxycillin for 5 days total per eTG 2024, based on evidence supporting shorter courses. Clinical improvement occurs within 3-7 days, but complete radiological resolution takes 4-6 weeks. Routine follow-up chest X-ray is unnecessary with satisfactory clinical response. This approach supports antimicrobial stewardship by minimising antibiotic exposure.

question.scenario: A 52-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 3-day history of fever, dry cough, myalgia, and headache. She has a documented severe penicillin allergy (previous anaphylaxis to amoxycillin). On examination, temperature is 38.6°C, heart rate 92 bpm, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Chest examination reveals scattered crackles in the left lower zone. Chest X-ray confirms left lower lobe pneumonia. CURB-65 score is 0. The GP decides to treat with doxycycline as first-line therapy due to the penicillin allergy.
question.stem: According to Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate doxycycline regimen for this patient with mild community-acquired pneumonia?

options.A: Doxycycline 200 mg orally as a loading dose, then 100 mg once daily for 4 days (total 5 days)
options.B: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days
options.C: Doxycycline 100 mg orally once daily for 7 days
options.D: Doxycycline 200 mg orally twice daily for 3 days

mcqs.explanation: According to eTG Complete and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic (2024), doxycycline for community-acquired pneumonia should be dosed at 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days in uncomplicated cases. This dosing provides adequate serum and tissue concentrations to cover common CAP pathogens including Streptococcus pneumoniae (when penicillin cannot be used) and atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila. Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic with excellent oral bioavailability (>90%) and tissue penetration, making it suitable for respiratory tract infections. While some sources recommend a loading dose of 200 mg on day 1 followed by 100 mg daily (option A), Australian Therapeutic Guidelines specify 100 mg twice daily dosing without a loading dose for pneumonia to ensure consistent therapeutic levels. The twice-daily dosing is preferred over once-daily (option C) for serious infections like pneumonia, as it maintains more consistent serum concentrations above the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for pneumococcal strains. Option D (200 mg twice daily for 3 days) represents excessive dosing that increases adverse effects (particularly gastrointestinal upset and photosensitivity) without improving efficacy, and the 3-day duration is too short for pneumonia. This patient's presentation with dry cough, myalgia, and headache alongside fever raises suspicion for atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma or Chlamydophila), which makes doxycycline an excellent choice beyond just being an alternative for penicillin allergy. Patients should be counselled about doxycycline adverse effects including nausea (take with food, but avoid dairy products which reduce absorption), photosensitivity (sun protection advised), and oesophageal irritation (take with water, remain upright for 30 minutes). The 5-day duration aligns with antimicrobial stewardship principles and evidence supporting shorter courses for uncomplicated CAP.
mcqs.summary: Doxycycline for mild CAP is dosed at 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days per eTG 2024. This regimen provides adequate coverage for typical pathogens (when penicillin contraindicated) and atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella). Twice-daily dosing maintains therapeutic levels. Counsel patients about photosensitivity and take with water to prevent oesophageal irritation.
citations: eTG Complete - Respiratory: Community-acquired pneumonia - Penicillin allergy (2024-2025)

Australian Medicines Handbook - Doxycycline (2024)

question.scenario: A 28-year-old university student presents with a 5-day history of gradual-onset fever, severe headache, myalgia, and non-productive cough. She has no significant past medical history and is not pregnant. On examination, temperature is 38.9°C, heart rate 96 bpm, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Chest examination reveals scattered crackles bilaterally but is otherwise unremarkable. Chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy infiltrates. Blood tests show normal white cell count (7.2 × 10⁹/L) with normal neutrophil count. The clinical picture is consistent with atypical community-acquired pneumonia, likely Mycoplasma pneumoniae. CURB-65 score is 0.
question.stem: According to Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, which macrolide antibiotic regimen is MOST appropriate for outpatient management of suspected atypical pneumonia in this patient?

options.A: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily for 3 days
options.B: Clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
options.C: Roxithromycin 300 mg orally once daily for 5 days
options.D: Erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 10 days

mcqs.explanation: For suspected atypical community-acquired pneumonia, particularly Mycoplasma pneumoniae, macrolide antibiotics are highly effective due to excellent activity against atypical organisms and convenient dosing. According to eTG Complete and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic (2024), azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily for 3 days is the preferred macrolide regimen for mild-to-moderate atypical pneumonia in Australia. Azithromycin has several advantages: (1) Excellent intracellular and tissue penetration with prolonged tissue half-life, allowing shorter treatment courses; (2) Once-daily dosing improves compliance; (3) Better gastrointestinal tolerability compared to erythromycin; (4) The 3-day course provides equivalent efficacy to longer courses due to azithromycin's pharmacokinetic properties (tissue concentrations remain therapeutic for 5-7 days after the last dose). This patient's presentation is classic for Mycoplasma pneumoniae: young adult, gradual onset, prominent constitutional symptoms (headache, myalgia), non-productive cough, bilateral infiltrates on CXR, and normal white cell count. While option B (clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days) is effective and listed in some international guidelines, it is not first-line in Australian Therapeutic Guidelines which favour azithromycin for convenience. Option C (roxithromycin) is less commonly used in Australia for pneumonia and has less robust evidence compared to azithromycin. Option D (erythromycin) is effective but poorly tolerated due to gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping) and requires four-times-daily dosing, making it a second-line choice. For hospitalised patients with atypical pneumonia or severe CAP requiring empirical coverage for both typical and atypical organisms, azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily is used in combination with benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone. The 3-day oral course is specifically for outpatient mild-to-moderate cases, which this patient represents with CURB-65 score 0.
mcqs.summary: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily for 3 days is first-line macrolide therapy for suspected atypical CAP (Mycoplasma) per eTG 2024. Advantages include excellent tissue penetration with prolonged half-life (therapeutic levels persist 5-7 days post-dose), once-daily dosing improving compliance, and better tolerability than erythromycin. Three-day course is adequate for mild-moderate outpatient cases.

question.scenario: A 68-year-old man is admitted to hospital with severe community-acquired pneumonia. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and ischaemic heart disease. On presentation, he is confused (AMTS 7/10), temperature 39.2°C, heart rate 118 bpm, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air (92% on 6L oxygen via Hudson mask). Chest examination reveals widespread crackles and bronchial breathing in the right lower and middle zones. Chest X-ray shows multilobar pneumonia involving right middle and lower lobes. Blood tests show: white cell count 18.2 × 10⁹/L, urea 11.4 mmol/L, creatinine 142 μmol/L. CURB-65 score is 5. Blood cultures and sputum cultures have been sent.
question.stem: According to Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate initial intravenous antibiotic regimen for this patient with severe community-acquired pneumonia?

options.A: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly plus doxycycline 100 mg IV 12-hourly
options.B: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily
options.C: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV 8-hourly plus vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg IV loading dose
options.D: Meropenem 1 g IV 8-hourly monotherapy

mcqs.explanation: This patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia with CURB-65 score 5, multilobar involvement, hypoxaemia, and hypotension requiring immediate hospital admission and consideration for intensive care unit assessment. According to eTG Complete and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic (2024), the first-line intravenous antibiotic regimen for severe CAP is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. This combination provides: (1) Broad-spectrum coverage of Streptococcus pneumoniae including penicillin-resistant strains via ceftriaxone (third-generation cephalosporin with excellent CNS and respiratory tract penetration); (2) Coverage of atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella) via azithromycin; (3) Potential synergistic benefit and improved outcomes in severe CAP demonstrated in observational studies, although the mechanism remains debated (immunomodulatory effects of macrolides vs. true antimicrobial synergy). The once-daily dosing of both agents is convenient and supported by pharmacokinetic data. Option A (benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline) is appropriate for moderate-severity CAP requiring hospitalisation but not for severe/ICU-level CAP, as benzylpenicillin may have inadequate activity against penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, and IV doxycycline availability is limited in many Australian hospitals. Option C (piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin) is excessive broad-spectrum coverage not indicated for community-acquired pneumonia; this regimen is appropriate for healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP) or hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) with risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which this patient does not have. Option D (meropenem monotherapy) is inappropriate for CAP; carbapenems are reserved for multidrug-resistant organisms and would not provide adequate atypical coverage. This patient requires supportive care including oxygen therapy (target SpO2 ≥92%), IV fluids for hypotension, and close monitoring with consideration for ICU admission given his high CURB-65 score and physiological instability.
mcqs.summary: Severe CAP (CURB-65 ≥3) requires IV therapy with ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus azithromycin 500 mg daily per eTG 2024. This combination covers penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical organisms (Legionella, Mycoplasma), with evidence supporting improved outcomes in severe cases. Once-daily dosing is convenient. Reserve broader regimens for healthcare-associated pneumonia with MRSA/Pseudomonas risk.

question.scenario: A 76-year-old nursing home resident is brought to the emergency department with fever, cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, and confusion. She has a history of previous stroke with residual dysphagia and requires a pureed diet. Carers report she had a choking episode 3 days ago during dinner. On examination, she is drowsy but rousable, temperature 38.8°C, heart rate 104 bpm, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 90% on room air. Chest examination reveals reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles in the right lower zone. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation with air-fluid level suggesting early abscess formation. Dental examination reveals poor dentition with multiple carious teeth and gingival disease.
question.stem: What is the MOST appropriate antibiotic regimen for this patient with suspected aspiration pneumonia according to Australian Therapeutic Guidelines?

options.A: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily monotherapy
options.B: Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV 4-hourly plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly
options.C: Amoxycillin-clavulanate 1.2 g IV 8-hourly
options.D: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV 8-hourly plus vancomycin 1.5 g IV 12-hourly

mcqs.explanation: This patient has classic aspiration pneumonia following a witnessed aspiration event in the context of dysphagia from previous stroke. Key features supporting aspiration pneumonia include: (1) History of stroke with dysphagia (major risk factor); (2) Witnessed choking episode; (3) Foul-smelling sputum (suggesting anaerobic infection); (4) Right lower lobe consolidation (gravity-dependent area in supine/semi-recumbent position); (5) Air-fluid level suggesting early lung abscess formation (complication of aspiration pneumonia); (6) Poor dental hygiene (source of oral anaerobes). According to eTG Complete and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic (2024), the first-line treatment for aspiration pneumonia requiring hospitalisation is benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV 4-hourly (or 2.4 g IV 4-hourly for severe cases) PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly. This combination provides: (1) Coverage of Streptococcus pneumoniae and other streptococci via benzylpenicillin; (2) Excellent anaerobic coverage via metronidazole (anaerobes from oral flora including Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, and Peptostreptococcus species are key pathogens in aspiration pneumonia). Metronidazole penetrates well into abscess cavities, making it ideal given the air-fluid level. Option C (amoxycillin-clavulanate) is an acceptable alternative that provides both aerobic and anaerobic coverage in a single agent, and is particularly useful for oral switch therapy or when compliance with two-drug regimen is problematic. However, benzylpenicillin plus metronidazole is listed as first-line in eTG for hospitalised patients as it provides superior anaerobic coverage with less risk of Clostridium difficile infection compared to amoxycillin-clavulanate. Option A (ceftriaxone monotherapy) is inadequate as it lacks anaerobic coverage, which is essential in aspiration pneumonia. Option D (piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin) is excessive broad-spectrum coverage appropriate for healthcare-associated or hospital-acquired pneumonia with MRSA and Pseudomonas risk, not community-onset aspiration pneumonia. This patient will also require dysphagia assessment (speech pathology), dental review, and measures to prevent recurrent aspiration (upright positioning during feeding, thickened fluids if appropriate).
mcqs.summary: Aspiration pneumonia requires anaerobic coverage due to oral flora. First-line therapy per eTG 2024 is benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV 4-hourly plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly. This combination covers Streptococcus pneumoniae and anaerobes (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium). Amoxycillin-clavulanate is an alternative. Key diagnostic features: dysphagia history, witnessed aspiration, foul sputum, dependent lung zone consolidation.

question.scenario: A 71-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, productive cough, and shortness of breath. He was discharged from hospital 3 weeks ago following admission for acute exacerbation of chronic heart failure. He also attends a haemodialysis unit three times weekly for end-stage renal disease. On examination, temperature is 38.9°C, heart rate 108 bpm, blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Chest examination reveals bibasal crackles and reduced air entry at the right base. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Blood tests show: white cell count 16.4 × 10⁹/L, urea 18.2 mmol/L, creatinine 412 μmol/L (baseline 380 μmol/L). He has no known drug allergies.
question.stem: This patient's pneumonia is classified as healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP). According to Australian guidelines, which feature distinguishes HCAP from typical community-acquired pneumonia and influences antibiotic selection?

options.A: HCAP requires routine coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in all cases
options.B: HCAP is associated with increased risk of multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA and Pseudomonas; antibiotic choice should be guided by local epidemiology and individual risk factors
options.C: HCAP should be treated identically to hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) with broad-spectrum antibiotics including vancomycin and meropenem
options.D: HCAP requires longer antibiotic duration (14-21 days) compared to community-acquired pneumonia (5-7 days)

mcqs.explanation: Healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP) is defined as pneumonia occurring in patients with recent healthcare contact, including: (1) Hospitalisation for ≥2 days in the preceding 90 days; (2) Residence in nursing home or long-term care facility; (3) Home infusion therapy, wound care, or haemodialysis within the preceding 30 days; (4) Attendance at hospital or haemodialysis clinic; or (5) Family member with multidrug-resistant organism. This patient meets multiple HCAP criteria: recent hospital admission (3 weeks ago) and regular haemodialysis attendance. According to eTG Complete and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic (2024), the key distinguishing feature of HCAP is increased risk of multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms, particularly methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, compared to typical community-acquired pneumonia. However, Australian guidelines emphasise that antibiotic selection should be individualised based on: (1) Local epidemiology (MRSA and Pseudomonas prevalence varies between institutions); (2) Individual patient risk factors (previous culture results, recent antibiotic exposure, severity of illness); (3) Clinical severity. Routine broad-spectrum coverage for all HCAP patients (option A) leads to unnecessary antibiotic use, increased costs, adverse effects (particularly C. difficile infection), and selection pressure for resistance. Option C is incorrect; while HCAP has overlapping features with hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), they are distinct entities and HCAP can often be managed with narrower-spectrum regimens if individual risk assessment suggests low MDR risk. For this patient, appropriate empirical therapy would be piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV 8-hourly (adjusted for renal impairment) to cover Pseudomonas given his haemodialysis attendance. MRSA coverage with vancomycin or linezolid should be considered if he has previous MRSA colonisation/infection, recent antibiotic exposure, or severe illness. Option D is incorrect; duration should be guided by clinical response (typically 5-7 days if responding well), not automatically prolonged.
mcqs.summary: Healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP) occurs in patients with recent healthcare contact (hospital admission <90 days, nursing home, haemodialysis). HCAP carries increased MDR organism risk (MRSA, Pseudomonas), but Australian guidelines recommend individualised antibiotic selection based on local epidemiology and patient risk factors, not routine broad-spectrum coverage. This approach balances effective treatment with antimicrobial stewardship.

question.scenario: A 58-year-old woman has been intubated and mechanically ventilated in the intensive care unit for 6 days following complicated abdominal surgery. She develops new fever to 39.1°C, increased purulent tracheal secretions, and worsening oxygenation requiring increased ventilator settings. Chest X-ray shows new right lower lobe infiltrate that was not present on admission. Tracheal aspirate Gram stain shows Gram-negative bacilli. Microbiological cultures are pending. She has received ceftriaxone for surgical prophylaxis in the perioperative period. The ICU team suspects ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP).
question.stem: According to Australian guidelines for ventilator-associated pneumonia, what is the MOST appropriate initial empirical antibiotic regimen pending culture results?

options.A: Continue ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as it provides adequate coverage for ventilator-associated pneumonia
options.B: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV 6-hourly (or 8-hourly with extended infusion) to cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other Gram-negative organisms
options.C: Meropenem 1 g IV 8-hourly plus vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg loading dose to cover carbapenem-resistant organisms and MRSA
options.D: Gentamicin 5-7 mg/kg IV daily monotherapy guided by therapeutic drug monitoring

mcqs.explanation: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is defined as pneumonia developing >48 hours after endotracheal intubation, and is a common and serious complication in mechanically ventilated patients. This patient meets diagnostic criteria for VAP with new fever, purulent tracheal secretions, new radiographic infiltrate, and worsening oxygenation after 6 days of mechanical ventilation. According to eTG Complete and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic (2024), the microbiology of VAP differs significantly from community-acquired pneumonia, with a predominance of Gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter species, as well as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). The first-line empirical therapy for VAP in Australian guidelines is piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV 6-hourly (or 8-hourly with extended infusion over 4 hours to optimise time-dependent killing). Piperacillin-tazobactam provides: (1) Excellent activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the most common and concerning pathogen in VAP; (2) Broad Gram-negative coverage including ESBL-producing organisms via the beta-lactamase inhibitor tazobactam; (3) Gram-positive coverage including methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Option A is incorrect; ceftriaxone (third-generation cephalosporin) has inadequate Pseudomonas activity and is inappropriate for VAP empirical therapy. Option C (meropenem plus vancomycin) represents maximal broad-spectrum therapy reserved for critically ill patients with septic shock, known colonisation with carbapenem-resistant organisms, or VAP in units with high rates of carbapenem resistance or MRSA. This patient does not currently require this level of escalation. Option D (gentamicin monotherapy) is inadequate; aminoglycosides have limited respiratory tract penetration and should not be used as monotherapy for pneumonia, although they may be added to beta-lactams for synergistic activity against Pseudomonas in severe cases. De-escalation based on culture and susceptibility results is a key antimicrobial stewardship principle—once organisms are identified, therapy should be narrowed to the most specific effective agent. If MRSA is suspected based on local epidemiology or previous cultures, vancomycin or linezolid should be added to piperacillin-tazobactam empirically.
mcqs.summary: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP, >48h post-intubation) requires empirical coverage for Gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa. First-line therapy per eTG 2024 is piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV 6-hourly. Reserve meropenem plus vancomycin for septic shock or known resistant organisms. De-escalate based on culture results following antimicrobial stewardship principles.
