Australian Rheumatology Association: Management of ILD in inflammatory myopathies (2024)
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Non-specific interstitial pneumonia and CTD-ILD (2024-2025)
Distler O et al. Nintedanib for Systemic Sclerosis-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease (SENSCIS trial). N Engl J Med. 2019
Tashkin DP et al. Mycophenolate mofetil versus oral cyclophosphamide in scleroderma-related interstitial lung disease (SLS II). Lancet Respir Med. 2016

learning_objectives: Recognition of NSIP pattern features (subpleural sparing key)
Immunosuppressive therapy as first-line for CTD-ILD with NSIP
Mycophenolate mofetil preferred over azathioprine in CTD-ILD
Differentiation from IPF (which does not respond to immunosuppression)
Understanding better prognosis of NSIP vs UIP pattern

question.scenario: A 52-year-old pigeon breeder presents with a 3-month history of progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. He keeps 20 racing pigeons in his backyard. Chest examination reveals fine bibasal crackles. Spirometry shows FVC 65% predicted with a restrictive pattern. High-resolution CT chest demonstrates diffuse centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation on inspiratory images, and air trapping on expiratory images. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial management?
question.stem: A 52-year-old pigeon breeder presents with a 3-month history of progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. He keeps 20 racing pigeons in his backyard. Chest examination reveals fine bibasal crackles. Spirometry shows FVC 65% predicted with a restrictive pattern. High-resolution CT chest demonstrates diffuse centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation on inspiratory images, and air trapping on expiratory images. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial management?

options.A: Commence prednisolone 50mg daily and continue pigeon breeding with mask protection
options.B: Complete avoidance of pigeon exposure and clinical reassessment in 4-6 weeks
options.C: Prescribe long-term azathioprine 2mg/kg daily as steroid-sparing agent
options.D: Arrange urgent bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy
options.E: Start pirfenidone 267mg three times daily for antifibrotic therapy

mcqs.explanation: This patient has classic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (bird fancier's lung) based on exposure history, subacute presentation, and characteristic HRCT findings (centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation, air trapping). The MOST important initial management is complete and permanent antigen avoidance. In many cases of acute/subacute hypersensitivity pneumonitis, antigen avoidance alone leads to clinical improvement within 4-6 weeks without need for corticosteroids. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 0.5-1mg/kg daily) are reserved for patients who fail to improve with antigen avoidance alone or have severe/progressive disease. Mask protection is insufficient—complete avoidance is required. Immunosuppressants like azathioprine are used only in chronic fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis unresponsive to steroids. Bronchoscopy may be needed if diagnosis unclear, but clinical picture and HRCT are highly suggestive. Pirfenidone is used for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, not hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
mcqs.summary: Bird fancier's lung is common in Australia due to pigeon racing hobby and backyard bird keeping. TSANZ guidelines emphasize antigen avoidance as first-line therapy. eTG Complete recommends corticosteroids only for progressive disease after failed antigen avoidance.

citations.evidence: Initial management of acute/subacute hypersensitivity pneumonitis involves complete avoidance of the causative antigen. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 0.5-1mg/kg) are indicated for severe symptoms or failure to improve with antigen avoidance after 4-6 weeks.
citations.relevance: Establishes antigen avoidance as first-line therapy before corticosteroids

citations.source: TSANZ Position Statement on Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (2020)
citations.evidence: HRCT findings of centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation, and air trapping are characteristic of subacute hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Complete and permanent antigen avoidance is the cornerstone of management.
citations.relevance: Confirms diagnostic HRCT pattern and primacy of antigen avoidance

citations.evidence: In hypersensitivity pneumonitis, corticosteroids are not always required if antigen avoidance leads to improvement. Reserve prednisolone for progressive or severe disease.
citations.relevance: Supports watchful waiting approach after antigen avoidance before initiating steroids

question.scenario: A 28-year-old Nigerian-Australian woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset ankle pain, bilateral leg rash, and dry cough over 2 weeks. She is otherwise well. Examination reveals tender, raised, erythematous nodules on both shins and bilateral ankle effusions. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal infiltrates. Spirometry is normal. Which of the following statements about her condition is MOST accurate?
question.stem: A 28-year-old Nigerian-Australian woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset ankle pain, bilateral leg rash, and dry cough over 2 weeks. She is otherwise well. Examination reveals tender, raised, erythematous nodules on both shins and bilateral ankle effusions. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal infiltrates. Spirometry is normal. Which of the following statements about her condition is MOST accurate?

options.A: She requires urgent commencement of prednisolone 0.5mg/kg daily to prevent progressive pulmonary fibrosis
options.B: Her presentation represents Stage II sarcoidosis with a 50% chance of spontaneous resolution
options.C: She has Löfgren syndrome with an excellent prognosis and >80% spontaneous remission rate
options.D: Bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound-guided lymph node biopsy is mandatory before treatment
options.E: She should be commenced on methotrexate 15mg weekly as first-line steroid-sparing therapy

mcqs.explanation: This patient has classic Löfgren syndrome, a distinct acute presentation of sarcoidosis characterized by the triad of: (1) bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, (2) erythema nodosum (tender shin nodules), and (3) polyarthritis (typically ankles). Löfgren syndrome has an excellent prognosis with >80% spontaneous remission within 2 years, particularly in women and those of African descent. Treatment is symptomatic only (NSAIDs for arthritis/erythema nodosum). Corticosteroids are NOT required for Löfgren syndrome as it is self-limiting. This represents Stage I sarcoidosis (hilar lymphadenopathy alone, without parenchymal infiltrates), which has 60-80% spontaneous resolution rate—Stage II (lymphadenopathy + infiltrates) has lower remission rates. Tissue biopsy is desirable but not mandatory when clinical presentation is classic for Löfgren syndrome. Methotrexate is used only as steroid-sparing agent in chronic progressive sarcoidosis requiring long-term immunosuppression.
mcqs.summary: Sarcoidosis has increased prevalence in African and Indigenous Australian populations. Löfgren syndrome is an important diagnosis to recognize in Australian emergency departments as it requires only symptomatic treatment (NSAIDs) rather than immunosuppression. eTG Complete emphasizes conservative management of acute sarcoidosis presentations.

citations.evidence: Löfgren syndrome (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, arthritis) is an acute form of sarcoidosis with excellent prognosis. Over 80% achieve spontaneous remission. Treatment is symptomatic with NSAIDs; corticosteroids are not required.
citations.relevance: Establishes diagnosis, excellent prognosis, and conservative management approach

citations.source: TSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Sarcoidosis (2021)
citations.evidence: Stage I sarcoidosis (isolated bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy) has 60-80% spontaneous resolution rate. Löfgren syndrome, a subset of Stage I, has even better prognosis (>80% remission). Systemic corticosteroids are reserved for progressive parenchymal disease or extrapulmonary organ involvement.
citations.relevance: Confirms staging, prognosis, and indications for corticosteroid therapy

citations.evidence: In Löfgren syndrome, tissue biopsy is not mandatory if clinical presentation is classic. Treatment is NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen 500mg twice daily) for symptomatic relief of arthritis and erythema nodosum.
citations.relevance: Supports clinical diagnosis without mandatory biopsy and NSAID therapy

question.scenario: A 45-year-old woman with biopsy-proven pulmonary sarcoidosis has been managed with prednisolone for 6 months. Her initial dose of 40mg daily was successfully tapered to 10mg daily, but each attempt to reduce below 10mg daily results in recurrent dyspnoea and worsening chest X-ray infiltrates. Her FVC has declined from 85% to 72% predicted. She has developed cushingoid features, hyperglycaemia (HbA1c 7.2%), and osteopaenia on DEXA scan. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next management step?
question.stem: A 45-year-old woman with biopsy-proven pulmonary sarcoidosis has been managed with prednisolone for 6 months. Her initial dose of 40mg daily was successfully tapered to 10mg daily, but each attempt to reduce below 10mg daily results in recurrent dyspnoea and worsening chest X-ray infiltrates. Her FVC has declined from 85% to 72% predicted. She has developed cushingoid features, hyperglycaemia (HbA1c 7.2%), and osteopaenia on DEXA scan. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next management step?

options.A: Continue prednisolone 10mg daily indefinitely as lowest effective maintenance dose
options.B: Increase prednisolone to 40mg daily and refer for lung transplant assessment
options.C: Add methotrexate 15mg weekly as steroid-sparing agent and gradually taper prednisolone
options.D: Switch to inhaled budesonide 800mcg twice daily to minimize systemic side effects
options.E: Commence azithromycin 250mg three times weekly as anti-inflammatory therapy

mcqs.explanation: This patient has steroid-dependent sarcoidosis with significant corticosteroid-related adverse effects (cushingoid features, hyperglycaemia, osteopaenia). When patients require >10mg prednisolone daily to control disease or develop significant steroid toxicity, steroid-sparing immunosuppressants should be added. Methotrexate is the most commonly used first-line steroid-sparing agent for pulmonary sarcoidosis (dose 10-25mg weekly, often starting at 15mg). Methotrexate allows gradual taper and reduction of prednisolone dose while maintaining disease control. Alternative steroid-sparing agents include azathioprine, mycophenolate, and leflunomide. Long-term prednisolone ≥10mg daily is associated with cumulative toxicity and should be avoided if possible. Increasing prednisolone would worsen side effects; transplant is reserved for end-stage fibrotic disease unresponsive to medical therapy. Inhaled corticosteroids are ineffective for parenchymal sarcoidosis. Azithromycin has limited evidence in sarcoidosis and is not standard therapy.
mcqs.summary: Methotrexate is PBS-subsidized for sarcoidosis in Australia when patients are steroid-dependent or develop significant steroid toxicity. eTG Complete and TSANZ guidelines recommend methotrexate as first-line steroid-sparing agent. Monitoring includes monthly FBC and LFTs for first 3 months, then 2-3 monthly.

citations.evidence: For patients requiring >10mg prednisolone daily or developing significant steroid toxicity, add steroid-sparing immunosuppressant. Methotrexate 10-25mg weekly is first-line steroid-sparing agent for pulmonary sarcoidosis. Monitor FBC, LFTs monthly initially.
citations.relevance: Establishes indication for steroid-sparing therapy and methotrexate as first-line agent

citations.source: TSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Sarcoidosis (2021)
citations.evidence: Steroid-dependent sarcoidosis (inability to taper below 10-15mg prednisolone or disease relapse on taper) is an indication for steroid-sparing immunosuppression. Methotrexate, azathioprine, and mycophenolate are effective options, with methotrexate having most evidence.
citations.relevance: Confirms definition of steroid-dependence and methotrexate as evidence-based choice

citations.evidence: Methotrexate 15-25mg orally once weekly is used as steroid-sparing agent in sarcoidosis. Start folic acid 5mg once weekly (day after methotrexate) to reduce toxicity. Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).
citations.relevance: Provides dosing, monitoring, and safety information for methotrexate in sarcoidosis

question.scenario: A 68-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation presents with 4 months of progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. He has been taking amiodarone 200mg daily for 3 years (total cumulative dose ~220g). He denies fever. Examination reveals bibasal crackles and oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral peripheral infiltrates. High-resolution CT chest demonstrates bilateral ground-glass opacification with areas of consolidation in upper and lower lobes. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 58% predicted and DLCO 48% predicted. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial management?
question.stem: A 68-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation presents with 4 months of progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. He has been taking amiodarone 200mg daily for 3 years (total cumulative dose ~220g). He denies fever. Examination reveals bibasal crackles and oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral peripheral infiltrates. High-resolution CT chest demonstrates bilateral ground-glass opacification with areas of consolidation in upper and lower lobes. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 58% predicted and DLCO 48% predicted. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial management?

options.A: Continue amiodarone and add prednisolone 50mg daily to treat interstitial lung disease
options.B: Cease amiodarone immediately, switch to sotalol, and commence prednisolone 1mg/kg daily
options.C: Reduce amiodarone dose to 100mg daily and monitor with serial pulmonary function tests
options.D: Continue amiodarone but add prophylactic co-trimoxazole for possible Pneumocystis pneumonia
options.E: Arrange urgent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage to exclude infection before ceasing amiodarone

mcqs.explanation: This patient has amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity, a serious adverse effect occurring in 5-15% of patients on chronic amiodarone therapy. Risk factors include cumulative dose >150g, daily dose >400mg, age >65 years, and duration >2 years. The MOST important initial management step is immediate cessation of amiodarone. Continuing or reducing the dose (rather than stopping) allows ongoing lung injury. Amiodarone has a very long half-life (~50 days), and lung toxicity may progress even after cessation. High-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 1mg/kg daily, typically 60-80mg) are recommended to suppress the inflammatory response, particularly in severe cases (hypoxia, extensive radiographic involvement, reduced DLCO). Alternative antiarrhythmic therapy (e.g., sotalol, flecainide) should be initiated if rhythm control is still required. While bronchoscopy with BAL may support diagnosis (foamy macrophages) and exclude infection, it should not delay cessation of amiodarone in a patient with high clinical suspicion.
mcqs.summary: Amiodarone is widely used in Australia for atrial fibrillation management. eTG Complete and TGA Product Information for amiodarone warn of pulmonary toxicity risk. Australian guidelines recommend baseline and 6-monthly pulmonary function tests (FVC, DLCO) and annual chest X-rays for patients on long-term amiodarone. PBS criteria for amiodarone require documentation of failure of other antiarrhythmics.

citations.evidence: Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity occurs in 5-15% of patients, particularly with cumulative doses >150g. Presents with dyspnoea, cough, hypoxia, and bilateral infiltrates on imaging. Management: immediate cessation of amiodarone and high-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 1mg/kg daily) for severe cases.
citations.relevance: Establishes diagnosis, risk factors, and management protocol for amiodarone lung toxicity

citations.evidence: Amiodarone has very long half-life (~50 days). Pulmonary toxicity may progress for weeks after cessation. Stop amiodarone immediately if pulmonary toxicity suspected. Consider prednisolone 40-60mg daily, tapering over 3-6 months. Monitor with serial chest X-rays and pulmonary function tests.
citations.relevance: Confirms immediate cessation requirement and corticosteroid dosing

citations.evidence: Pulmonary toxicity is a serious adverse effect of amiodarone. Risk increases with cumulative dose and duration. Baseline and regular monitoring (chest X-ray annually, pulmonary function tests 6-monthly) recommended. Discontinue amiodarone if pulmonary toxicity develops.
citations.relevance: Australian regulatory guidance on monitoring and management of amiodarone pulmonary toxicity

question.scenario: A 72-year-old man with recurrent ventricular tachycardia is being commenced on amiodarone 200mg daily by the cardiology team. He has no pre-existing lung disease and is an ex-smoker (30 pack-years, ceased 10 years ago). Baseline chest X-ray is clear. Which of the following monitoring strategies is MOST appropriate for early detection of amiodarone pulmonary toxicity?
question.stem: A 72-year-old man with recurrent ventricular tachycardia is being commenced on amiodarone 200mg daily by the cardiology team. He has no pre-existing lung disease and is an ex-smoker (30 pack-years, ceased 10 years ago). Baseline chest X-ray is clear. Which of the following monitoring strategies is MOST appropriate for early detection of amiodarone pulmonary toxicity?

options.A: Chest X-ray every 3 months and pulmonary function tests (FVC, DLCO) every 6 months
options.B: High-resolution CT chest at baseline, 6 months, and annually thereafter
options.C: Pulmonary function tests (FVC, DLCO) at baseline and every 6 months; chest X-ray annually
options.D: Serial serum KL-6 (Krebs von den Lungen-6) levels monthly as biomarker of lung injury
options.E: Clinical assessment only; imaging and pulmonary function tests only if symptoms develop

mcqs.explanation: The recommended monitoring strategy for amiodarone pulmonary toxicity in Australia (per eTG Complete, AMH, and TGA Product Information) is: (1) Baseline pulmonary function tests (FVC, DLCO) and chest X-ray before starting amiodarone, (2) Pulmonary function tests every 6 months, and (3) Chest X-ray annually. A decline in DLCO (>15-20% from baseline) or FVC (>10-15%) may indicate early pulmonary toxicity before symptoms or radiographic changes appear. DLCO is particularly sensitive as it decreases earlier than FVC in interstitial lung disease. Annual chest X-ray detects established infiltrates. This monitoring schedule balances early detection with cost-effectiveness and radiation exposure. High-resolution CT is NOT routinely recommended for monitoring (reserved for diagnostic evaluation when toxicity suspected). Serum KL-6 is not validated or available in routine Australian practice. Clinical assessment alone misses subclinical toxicity, which is reversible if detected early.
mcqs.summary: Australian TGA Product Information for amiodarone mandates baseline and regular monitoring for pulmonary toxicity. Pulmonary function tests are bulk-billed under Medicare when performed for amiodarone monitoring (Item 11506). TSANZ guidelines recommend 6-monthly pulmonary function tests and annual chest X-rays for all patients on chronic amiodarone therapy.

citations.evidence: Before commencing amiodarone: baseline chest X-ray and pulmonary function tests (FVC, DLCO). During treatment: pulmonary function tests every 6 months and chest X-ray annually. Investigate promptly if patient develops dyspnoea, cough, or pulmonary function deterioration.
citations.relevance: Australian regulatory guidance on mandatory monitoring for amiodarone therapy

citations.evidence: Monitor for pulmonary toxicity with clinical assessment, chest X-ray annually, and pulmonary function tests (FVC, DLCO) 6-monthly. A decline in DLCO >15% from baseline warrants investigation for possible pulmonary toxicity.
citations.relevance: Establishes monitoring schedule and threshold for concern (DLCO decline >15%)

citations.evidence: Baseline and 6-monthly pulmonary function tests (including DLCO) are recommended. DLCO is more sensitive than chest X-ray for early detection of amiodarone pulmonary toxicity. Annual chest X-ray also recommended.
citations.relevance: Confirms superiority of DLCO for early detection and monitoring frequency

question.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been taking methotrexate 20mg weekly for 18 months with good disease control. She presents with 1 week of fever (38.5°C), dry cough, and progressive dyspnoea. She is taking folic acid 5mg weekly and has normal liver and renal function. Examination reveals oxygen saturation 88% on room air and diffuse crackles bilaterally. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. High-resolution CT chest demonstrates ground-glass opacification throughout both lungs. Which of the following is the MOST important immediate management step?
question.stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been taking methotrexate 20mg weekly for 18 months with good disease control. She presents with 1 week of fever (38.5°C), dry cough, and progressive dyspnoea. She is taking folic acid 5mg weekly and has normal liver and renal function. Examination reveals oxygen saturation 88% on room air and diffuse crackles bilaterally. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. High-resolution CT chest demonstrates ground-glass opacification throughout both lungs. Which of the following is the MOST important immediate management step?

options.A: Continue methotrexate but add prophylactic co-trimoxazole 960mg three times weekly
options.B: Cease methotrexate immediately and commence high-dose prednisolone 1mg/kg daily
options.C: Increase folic acid to 5mg daily to reverse methotrexate toxicity
options.D: Reduce methotrexate dose to 10mg weekly and add hydroxychloroquine 400mg daily
options.E: Administer folinic acid (leucovorin) 15mg IV six-hourly as specific antidote

mcqs.explanation: This patient has acute methotrexate pneumonitis, a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of methotrexate therapy occurring in 5-10% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate. It can occur at any time during treatment (early or late) and at any dose (even low-dose weekly regimens). Clinical features include acute/subacute onset of fever, dry cough, dyspnoea, and hypoxia with diffuse infiltrates on imaging. The MOST important immediate step is cessation of methotrexate to prevent further lung injury. High-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 1mg/kg daily, typically 60-80mg) are the mainstay of treatment and should be commenced urgently. Mortality is 10-20% if untreated but improves significantly with early cessation and steroid therapy. Differential diagnosis includes infection (particularly Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, PJP) and underlying rheumatoid lung disease. However, acute presentation with fever and diffuse ground-glass opacification favours methotrexate pneumonitis over chronic rheumatoid ILD. Bronchoscopy with BAL may help exclude infection if diagnosis uncertain, but should not delay cessation of methotrexate and steroid initiation if clinical suspicion is high. Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used for methotrexate overdose or severe toxicity (e.g., pancytopenia, mucositis) but is NOT standard treatment for pneumonitis—high-dose corticosteroids are the primary therapy. Folic acid supplementation does not prevent or treat methotrexate pneumonitis.
mcqs.summary: Methotrexate is widely used in Australia for rheumatoid arthritis (PBS-subsidized). Australian TGA Product Information warns of rare but serious pulmonary toxicity. eTG Complete recommends patient education about symptoms of pneumonitis (fever, dry cough, breathlessness) and urgent review if these develop. Shared care arrangements between rheumatology and general practice require clear protocols for managing methotrexate toxicity.

citations.source: eTG Complete - Rheumatology, Methotrexate Adverse Effects
citations.evidence: Methotrexate pneumonitis is a rare (5-10% in RA patients) but potentially fatal complication. Presents acutely with fever, dry cough, dyspnoea, and bilateral infiltrates. Management: immediate cessation of methotrexate and high-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 1mg/kg daily). Exclude infection before attributing to drug.
citations.relevance: Establishes diagnosis, clinical features, and urgent management protocol

citations.evidence: Pulmonary toxicity from methotrexate can occur at any time and any dose. Stop methotrexate immediately if pneumonitis suspected. Treat with high-dose corticosteroids. Mortality 10-20% if treatment delayed. Leucovorin (folinic acid) is used for overdose/toxicity causing bone marrow suppression, not routinely for pneumonitis.
citations.relevance: Confirms immediate cessation requirement and corticosteroid therapy as primary treatment

citations.evidence: Acute methotrexate-induced pneumonitis is characterised by fever, cough, dyspnoea, and pulmonary infiltrates. Discontinue methotrexate if pneumonitis suspected. Corticosteroids may be beneficial. Exclude infection (including Pneumocystis) as differential diagnosis.
citations.relevance: Australian regulatory guidance on recognition and management of methotrexate pneumonitis

question.scenario: A 76-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections has been taking nitrofurantoin 50mg daily for prophylaxis for the past 2 years. She presents with 6 months of progressive dyspnoea on exertion. She denies fever or acute illness. Examination reveals bilateral fine crackles and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. High-resolution CT chest shows bilateral lower zone reticular changes and subpleural fibrosis. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 62% predicted and DLCO 54% predicted with restrictive pattern. Which of the following statements about her condition is MOST accurate?
question.stem: A 76-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections has been taking nitrofurantoin 50mg daily for prophylaxis for the past 2 years. She presents with 6 months of progressive dyspnoea on exertion. She denies fever or acute illness. Examination reveals bilateral fine crackles and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. High-resolution CT chest shows bilateral lower zone reticular changes and subpleural fibrosis. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 62% predicted and DLCO 54% predicted with restrictive pattern. Which of the following statements about her condition is MOST accurate?

options.A: This represents acute nitrofurantoin pneumonitis and will resolve completely within 2 weeks of ceasing the drug
options.B: This is chronic nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary fibrosis which may be irreversible despite drug cessation
options.C: High-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 1mg/kg daily) will reverse the pulmonary fibrosis
options.D: She can safely continue nitrofurantoin as the lung changes are due to underlying idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
options.E: Switching from nitrofurantoin to trimethoprim will allow continued UTI prophylaxis without further lung injury

mcqs.explanation: This patient has chronic nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, a serious and often irreversible complication of long-term nitrofurantoin use (typically >6 months, particularly in elderly women on prophylactic therapy). Nitrofurantoin can cause two distinct patterns of lung injury: (1) Acute pneumonitis (onset hours to weeks, presents with fever, cough, dyspnoea, bilateral infiltrates, peripheral eosinophilia; resolves rapidly after drug cessation), or (2) Chronic pulmonary fibrosis (insidious onset over months to years, presents with progressive dyspnoea, crackles, reticular changes/fibrosis on HRCT; often irreversible). This patient's 6-month progressive course, absence of fever, and HRCT showing fibrosis (not ground-glass) indicate chronic disease. The MOST important management step is immediate and permanent cessation of nitrofurantoin. Some patients stabilize after cessation, but established fibrosis typically does not reverse. Corticosteroids have limited efficacy in chronic nitrofurantoin fibrosis (unlike acute pneumonitis where they may help). Continuing nitrofurantoin will lead to progressive and potentially fatal pulmonary fibrosis. Alternative UTI prophylaxis (e.g., trimethoprim, cranberry) should be used, but switching after fibrosis has developed does not reverse established lung injury—the fibrosis may be permanent.
mcqs.summary: Nitrofurantoin is widely used for UTI prophylaxis in Australia (PBS-subsidized). TGA has issued safety alerts about pulmonary toxicity risk, particularly with long-term use in elderly patients. eTG Complete recommends limiting nitrofurantoin prophylaxis duration and monitoring for respiratory symptoms. Australian Medicines Handbook advises against long-term nitrofurantoin in elderly due to pulmonary fibrosis risk.

citations.source: eTG Complete - Urinary Tract Infections, Nitrofurantoin
citations.evidence: Nitrofurantoin can cause acute pneumonitis (onset hours-weeks, reversible) or chronic pulmonary fibrosis (insidious onset, may be irreversible). Chronic toxicity occurs with prolonged use (>6 months), particularly in elderly women. Presents with progressive dyspnoea and pulmonary fibrosis on imaging. Cease nitrofurantoin immediately; fibrosis may not reverse.
citations.relevance: Distinguishes acute vs chronic nitrofurantoin lung disease and establishes irreversibility of chronic form

citations.evidence: Chronic nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary fibrosis can be irreversible. Risk increases with duration of therapy (especially >6 months) and in elderly patients. Avoid long-term nitrofurantoin for UTI prophylaxis in elderly. Monitor for respiratory symptoms; cease immediately if develop.
citations.relevance: Confirms irreversibility and recommendation against long-term use in elderly

citations.source: TGA Medicines Safety Update - Nitrofurantoin and Pulmonary Reactions (2019)
citations.evidence: Nitrofurantoin-associated chronic pulmonary reactions can result in pulmonary fibrosis that may be irreversible. Risk factors include prolonged therapy and older age. Healthcare professionals should monitor patients on long-term nitrofurantoin for respiratory symptoms. Consider alternative UTI prophylaxis.
citations.relevance: Australian regulatory safety alert confirming irreversible fibrosis risk with long-term use

question.scenario: A 52-year-old woman with a 5-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with 9 months of progressive dyspnoea. She has been taking methotrexate 20mg weekly for 3 years with good joint disease control. Recent pulmonary function tests show FVC 68% predicted and DLCO 52% predicted. High-resolution CT chest demonstrates bilateral subpleural reticular opacities with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, predominantly in the lower lobes. The pattern is consistent with usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). Which of the following statements about her prognosis and management is MOST accurate?
question.stem: A 52-year-old woman with a 5-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with 9 months of progressive dyspnoea. She has been taking methotrexate 20mg weekly for 3 years with good joint disease control. Recent pulmonary function tests show FVC 68% predicted and DLCO 52% predicted. High-resolution CT chest demonstrates bilateral subpleural reticular opacities with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, predominantly in the lower lobes. The pattern is consistent with usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). Which of the following statements about her prognosis and management is MOST accurate?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated UIP has similar prognosis to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and should be treated with antifibrotic therapy
options.B: The UIP pattern indicates methotrexate pneumonitis and requires immediate cessation of methotrexate and high-dose corticosteroids
options.C: Rheumatoid ILD with NSIP pattern has better prognosis than UIP pattern; she requires lung transplant assessment
options.D: High-dose prednisolone 60mg daily will reverse the pulmonary fibrosis and improve lung function
options.E: This represents acute exacerbation of rheumatoid arthritis requiring escalation to biologic therapy (anti-TNF)

mcqs.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) can present with two main histopathological patterns: UIP and NSIP. RA-ILD with UIP pattern has worse prognosis than NSIP pattern and is similar to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) in terms of disease progression and survival (median survival 3-5 years). This patient's HRCT shows classic UIP features (subpleural/basal reticular opacities, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis) indicating progressive fibrotic disease. Recent evidence (INBUILD trial, 2019) supports use of antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib) for progressive fibrosing ILD including RA-ILD with UIP pattern, as it slows decline in FVC. Pirfenidone is also used off-label. Methotrexate pneumonitis presents acutely/subacutely (days to weeks) with fever, ground-glass opacities, and cellular infiltrates on HRCT—not chronic progressive UIP pattern. Immunosuppression (prednisolone, azathioprine, mycophenolate) may benefit NSIP pattern but has limited efficacy in established UIP fibrosis. High-dose corticosteroids do not reverse established fibrosis. Lung transplant is considered for end-stage disease unresponsive to medical therapy in suitable candidates.
mcqs.summary: Nintedanib is PBS-subsidized in Australia for IPF and progressive fibrosing ILD (including RA-ILD). TSANZ guidelines recommend antifibrotic therapy for RA-ILD with UIP pattern showing progression. Multidisciplinary discussion (respirology, rheumatology) is essential for management. eTG Complete recognizes worse prognosis of RA-UIP compared to RA-NSIP.

citations.source: eTG Complete - Respiratory, Connective Tissue Disease-ILD
citations.evidence: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated ILD with UIP pattern has poor prognosis similar to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (median survival 3-5 years). NSIP pattern has better prognosis. Consider antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib, pirfenidone) for progressive RA-ILD with UIP pattern.
citations.relevance: Establishes prognostic difference between UIP and NSIP patterns and role of antifibrotic therapy

citations.evidence: Progressive fibrosing ILD, including connective tissue disease-associated ILD with UIP pattern, should be considered for antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib) if showing evidence of progression (declining FVC, worsening symptoms, radiographic progression). Immunosuppression has limited benefit in established UIP fibrosis.
citations.relevance: Supports antifibrotic therapy for progressive RA-ILD with UIP pattern

citations.evidence: Nintedanib is PBS-subsidized for progressive fibrosing interstitial lung disease (PF-ILD) including connective tissue disease-associated ILD showing progression within 24 months (decline in FVC ≥10% predicted or decline in FVC 5-10% predicted plus worsening symptoms or HRCT progression).
citations.relevance: Australian funding criteria for antifibrotic therapy in RA-ILD

question.scenario: A 65-year-old man with seropositive (RF+, anti-CCP+) rheumatoid arthritis for 10 years presents for routine follow-up. He is asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective but mentions occasional dry cough. Examination reveals bibasal fine crackles that were not present 12 months ago. You arrange high-resolution CT chest which shows early bilateral subpleural reticular opacities without honeycombing. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 78% predicted (down from 88% one year ago) and DLCO 68% predicted. Which of the following management strategies is MOST appropriate at this stage?
question.stem: A 65-year-old man with seropositive (RF+, anti-CCP+) rheumatoid arthritis for 10 years presents for routine follow-up. He is asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective but mentions occasional dry cough. Examination reveals bibasal fine crackles that were not present 12 months ago. You arrange high-resolution CT chest which shows early bilateral subpleural reticular opacities without honeycombing. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 78% predicted (down from 88% one year ago) and DLCO 68% predicted. Which of the following management strategies is MOST appropriate at this stage?

options.A: Reassure patient that mild RA-ILD is common and requires no specific treatment; continue methotrexate
options.B: Cease methotrexate immediately as it may worsen RA-ILD and switch to hydroxychloroquine monotherapy
options.C: Commence mycophenolate mofetil 1g twice daily as first-line therapy for early RA-ILD
options.D: Initiate close monitoring (6-monthly pulmonary function tests, annual HRCT) and consider immunosuppression if progression occurs
options.E: Start pirfenidone 267mg three times daily immediately to prevent progression to end-stage fibrosis

mcqs.explanation: This patient has early, asymptomatic rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) detected on screening. RA-ILD occurs in 10-20% of RA patients and is a leading cause of mortality. Management of early, asymptomatic RA-ILD is controversial. Current evidence supports: (1) Close monitoring with serial pulmonary function tests (6-monthly) and HRCT imaging (annually or if progression suspected) to detect progression early, and (2) Initiating immunosuppressive therapy if progression occurs (declining FVC >10%, worsening symptoms, or radiographic progression). For progressive RA-ILD, options include mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or cyclophosphamide. Antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib) is reserved for progressive fibrosing ILD. The role of methotrexate in RA-ILD is debated—some studies suggest methotrexate does not worsen pre-existing RA-ILD and may even be protective. Current consensus is that methotrexate can be cautiously continued in stable RA-ILD with close monitoring, as joint disease control is also important. Ceasing methotrexate is considered if acute decline occurs. Starting aggressive immunosuppression (mycophenolate) or antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone) immediately in asymptomatic, stable disease is not standard—treatment escalation should be reserved for progressive disease.
mcqs.summary: TSANZ guidelines recommend screening for ILD in RA patients with respiratory symptoms or examination findings (crackles). Once RA-ILD diagnosed, close monitoring is essential. Mycophenolate and nintedanib are PBS-subsidized for progressive ILD. Multidisciplinary discussion (respiratory, rheumatology) guides treatment decisions for RA-ILD in Australia.

citations.evidence: Connective tissue disease-associated ILD requires monitoring for progression. Serial pulmonary function tests (every 3-6 months) and HRCT imaging (annually or if clinical concern) recommended. Initiate immunosuppressive therapy (mycophenolate, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide) if evidence of progression (declining FVC ≥10%, worsening symptoms, radiographic progression).
citations.relevance: Establishes monitoring strategy and criteria for treatment escalation

citations.evidence: Methotrexate can be cautiously continued in patients with stable RA-ILD under close respiratory monitoring, as recent evidence suggests it may not worsen pre-existing ILD. Cease methotrexate if acute respiratory deterioration occurs. Consider alternative DMARDs or biologics if methotrexate contraindicated.
citations.relevance: Supports cautious continuation of methotrexate in stable RA-ILD with monitoring

citations.evidence: For progressive RA-ILD, immunosuppressive therapy (mycophenolate 1-1.5g twice daily, azathioprine 2-3mg/kg daily, or cyclophosphamide) may slow progression. Antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib) is used for progressive fibrosing ILD. Close monitoring (pulmonary function tests, HRCT) essential to detect progression.
citations.relevance: Outlines treatment options for progressive RA-ILD and importance of monitoring

question.scenario: A 48-year-old woman with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc, previously called CREST syndrome) presents with 6 months of worsening dyspnoea on exertion. She has Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and anti-centromere antibodies. High-resolution CT chest shows bilateral ground-glass opacities and reticular changes with subpleural sparing. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 64% predicted and DLCO 48% predicted. Right heart catheterisation shows mean pulmonary artery pressure 32mmHg. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate treatment approach?
question.stem: A 48-year-old woman with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc, previously called CREST syndrome) presents with 6 months of worsening dyspnoea on exertion. She has Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and anti-centromere antibodies. High-resolution CT chest shows bilateral ground-glass opacities and reticular changes with subpleural sparing. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 64% predicted and DLCO 48% predicted. Right heart catheterisation shows mean pulmonary artery pressure 32mmHg. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate treatment approach?

options.A: Commence high-dose prednisolone 1mg/kg daily as first-line therapy for scleroderma-ILD
options.B: Start mycophenolate mofetil 1.5g twice daily and monitor with serial pulmonary function tests
options.C: Initiate bosentan 125mg twice daily for pulmonary arterial hypertension as primary problem
options.D: Arrange urgent lung transplant assessment as scleroderma-ILD has very poor prognosis
options.E: Commence nintedanib 150mg twice daily as scleroderma-ILD is a progressive fibrosing disease

mcqs.explanation: Systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD) is the leading cause of death in scleroderma, occurring in 40-75% of patients. The HRCT pattern typically shows non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) with ground-glass opacities and reticular changes, often with subpleural sparing (unlike UIP which is subpleural predominant). This patient has evidence of active, symptomatic ILD (dyspnoea, restrictive physiology with reduced DLCO). Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is now considered first-line therapy for SSc-ILD based on the SENSCIS and SLS-II trials, which showed MMF (1.5g twice daily) slows decline in FVC and is better tolerated than cyclophosphamide. Cyclophosphamide is an alternative for severe/rapidly progressive disease. High-dose corticosteroids are avoided in scleroderma as they increase risk of scleroderma renal crisis. This patient also has mild pulmonary hypertension (mPAP 32mmHg, threshold for PAH is ≥25mmHg in older definitions, ≥20mmHg in 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines), but the predominant issue is ILD (low DLCO can be from both ILD and PAH). Pulmonary vasodilator therapy (bosentan, sildenafil) is used for confirmed severe PAH (mPAP >25mmHg with elevated PVR) but should not be primary therapy when ILD is predominant. Nintedanib is PBS-approved for progressive fibrosing ILD but MMF is first-line for SSc-ILD.
mcqs.summary: Mycophenolate is PBS-subsidized for systemic sclerosis-associated ILD in Australia (Authority required). TSANZ and Australian Scleroderma Interest Group recommend MMF as first-line for SSc-ILD. Patients require monitoring (FBC, LFTs monthly initially, then 2-3 monthly). Scleroderma centres in major Australian cities provide multidisciplinary care (rheumatology, respiratory, cardiology).

citations.source: eTG Complete - Rheumatology, Systemic Sclerosis ILD
citations.evidence: Mycophenolate mofetil (1.5g twice daily) is first-line therapy for systemic sclerosis-associated ILD. It slows decline in FVC and is better tolerated than cyclophosphamide. Avoid high-dose corticosteroids (>15mg prednisolone daily) due to risk of scleroderma renal crisis. Monitor with serial pulmonary function tests every 3-6 months.
citations.relevance: Establishes MMF as first-line therapy and avoidance of high-dose steroids

citations.evidence: Systemic sclerosis-associated ILD typically shows NSIP pattern on HRCT. Mycophenolate mofetil is recommended first-line immunosuppressive therapy. Cyclophosphamide is alternative for severe/rapidly progressive disease. Nintedanib may be considered for progressive fibrosing phenotype unresponsive to immunosuppression.
citations.relevance: Confirms MMF as first-line and NSIP as typical pattern in SSc-ILD

citations.evidence: Mycophenolate is PBS-subsidized for systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease (Authority required). Dose: 1-1.5g twice daily. Criteria: diagnosed SSc-ILD with evidence of active disease (declining FVC, worsening symptoms, or radiographic progression).
citations.relevance: Australian funding criteria and dosing for mycophenolate in SSc-ILD

She denies joint pain or rash. High-resolution CT chest shows multiple small centrilobular nodules, patchy ground-glass opacities, and multiple small thin-walled cysts scattered throughout both lungs. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 72% predicted, FEV1 68% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.78, and DLCO 62% predicted. Which of the following is the MOST likely pulmonary manifestation of her Sjögren syndrome?
question.stem: A 55-year-old woman with primary Sjögren syndrome (dry eyes, dry mouth, positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies) presents with 3 months of dry cough and exertional dyspnoea. She denies joint pain or rash. High-resolution CT chest shows multiple small centrilobular nodules, patchy ground-glass opacities, and multiple small thin-walled cysts scattered throughout both lungs. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 72% predicted, FEV1 68% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.78, and DLCO 62% predicted. Which of the following is the MOST likely pulmonary manifestation of her Sjögren syndrome?

options.A: Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern progressing to pulmonary fibrosis
options.B: Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (LIP) with cystic changes
options.C: Follicular bronchiolitis with small airway disease
options.D: Organising pneumonia (previously called BOOP) requiring corticosteroids
options.E: Pulmonary amyloidosis with nodular lung disease

mcqs.explanation: Primary Sjögren syndrome can cause various pulmonary manifestations, with the most characteristic being lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (LIP). LIP is a rare form of interstitial lung disease characterized by diffuse infiltration of the lung interstitium and alveolar spaces by lymphocytes, plasma cells, and other lymphoid cells. HRCT features of LIP include: (1) ground-glass opacities, (2) centrilobular nodules, (3) thin-walled cysts (present in 60-80% of cases, a distinguishing feature from other ILDs), and (4) septal and bronchovascular bundle thickening. Pulmonary function tests typically show restrictive or mixed pattern with reduced DLCO. LIP in Sjögren syndrome has variable prognosis—some cases remain stable, others progress, and some respond to corticosteroids or immunosuppression. Follicular bronchiolitis (small airway inflammation with lymphoid follicles) also occurs in Sjögren syndrome and may coexist with LIP, but the presence of multiple thin-walled cysts is more characteristic of LIP. UIP pattern is uncommon in Sjögren lung disease. Organising pneumonia presents with consolidation/ground-glass opacities but not cysts. Pulmonary amyloidosis can cause nodules but is rare and presents differently.
mcqs.summary: Sjögren syndrome affects approximately 0.5-1% of Australians, predominantly women. Pulmonary involvement occurs in 10-20% of cases. TSANZ guidelines recognize LIP as characteristic pulmonary manifestation of Sjögren syndrome. Multidisciplinary ILD team assessment is recommended. Corticosteroids +/- immunosuppression used for progressive disease.

citations.source: eTG Complete - Rheumatology, Sjögren Syndrome Pulmonary Manifestations
citations.evidence: Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (LIP) is a characteristic pulmonary manifestation of primary Sjögren syndrome. HRCT shows ground-glass opacities, centrilobular nodules, and thin-walled cysts (distinguishing feature). Treatment with corticosteroids +/- immunosuppression (azathioprine, cyclophosphamide) for progressive disease.
citations.relevance: Establishes LIP as characteristic Sjögren lung manifestation with diagnostic HRCT features

citations.evidence: Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (LIP) is seen in autoimmune conditions, particularly Sjögren syndrome and HIV. HRCT features include ground-glass opacities, centrilobular nodules, and multiple thin-walled cysts (present in majority of cases). Cystic changes help distinguish LIP from other interstitial lung diseases.
citations.relevance: Confirms cystic changes as key distinguishing feature of LIP on HRCT

citations.evidence: Pulmonary manifestations of Sjögren syndrome include lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia, follicular bronchiolitis, and NSIP. LIP presents with cystic lung disease on HRCT. Treatment depends on severity: observation for mild disease, corticosteroids for symptomatic/progressive disease, immunosuppression (azathioprine, cyclophosphamide) for severe cases.
citations.relevance: Provides treatment approach for LIP in Sjögren syndrome based on disease severity

question.scenario: A 42-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of rapidly progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, and fever. She has also developed proximal muscle weakness and a heliotrope rash over her eyelids. Blood tests show elevated CK (2400 U/L), positive anti-MDA5 antibody, and normal anti-Jo1. High-resolution CT chest shows diffuse ground-glass opacities bilaterally with areas of consolidation. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 52% predicted and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
question.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of rapidly progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, and fever. She has also developed proximal muscle weakness and a heliotrope rash over her eyelids. Blood tests show elevated CK (2400 U/L), positive anti-MDA5 antibody, and normal anti-Jo1. High-resolution CT chest shows diffuse ground-glass opacities bilaterally with areas of consolidation. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 52% predicted and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Start pirfenidone 267mg three times daily for rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease
options.B: Commence pulse methylprednisolone 1g IV daily for 3 days followed by high-dose oral prednisolone and consider rituximab
options.C: Arrange urgent lung biopsy to confirm dermatomyositis-associated ILD before starting treatment
options.D: Initiate mycophenolate mofetil 1g twice daily and prednisolone 20mg daily as first-line combination
options.E: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam) for presumed severe community-acquired pneumonia

mcqs.explanation: This patient has dermatomyositis-associated interstitial lung disease (DM-ILD) with rapidly progressive course, indicated by anti-MDA5 (melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5) antibody positivity. Anti-MDA5 antibody is associated with clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (minimal muscle involvement) and rapidly progressive ILD, which has high mortality (up to 50% at 6 months) without aggressive treatment. The clinical presentation (skin rash, muscle weakness, elevated CK, rapidly progressive ILD with ground-glass opacities) is highly suggestive of DM-ILD, making lung biopsy unnecessary and potentially dangerous in an unstable patient. Urgent aggressive immunosuppression is required to prevent respiratory failure and death. First-line treatment for rapidly progressive DM-ILD consists of: (1) High-dose corticosteroids (pulse methylprednisolone 0.5-1g IV daily for 3 days, followed by oral prednisolone 1mg/kg daily), PLUS (2) Additional immunosuppression—options include cyclophosphamide IV, rituximab, tacrolimus, or mycophenolate. Rituximab is increasingly used for anti-MDA5-positive DM-ILD. Plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) may be added for refractory cases. Starting with oral prednisolone 20mg or mycophenolate alone is inadequate for life-threatening rapidly progressive disease. Antibiotics should be considered to cover possible superimposed infection, but primary treatment must be immunosuppression. Pirfenidone is for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, not inflammatory myositis-ILD.
mcqs.summary: Dermatomyositis-associated ILD is a rheumatological emergency requiring urgent rheumatology and respiratory consultation. Anti-MDA5 antibody testing is available through major Australian pathology laboratories. Pulse methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab are PBS-subsidized for severe autoimmune disease. ICU admission may be required for respiratory support. Multidisciplinary care in tertiary centres is essential.

citations.evidence: Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease in dermatomyositis (particularly anti-MDA5 antibody-positive) is a medical emergency with high mortality. Urgent treatment: pulse methylprednisolone 0.5-1g IV daily for 3 days, followed by high-dose oral prednisolone 1mg/kg daily, PLUS additional immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, rituximab, tacrolimus, or mycophenolate). Consider IVIg or plasma exchange for refractory cases.
citations.relevance: Establishes urgency and aggressive immunosuppression protocol for anti-MDA5 positive DM-ILD

citations.evidence: Anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis is associated with rapidly progressive ILD and high mortality. Clinical presentation (heliotrope rash, muscle weakness, rapidly progressive dyspnoea, ground-glass opacities on HRCT) is diagnostic; lung biopsy not required. Urgent combination immunosuppression (high-dose corticosteroids + cyclophosphamide/rituximab) is life-saving.
citations.relevance: Confirms clinical diagnosis without biopsy and need for combination immunosuppression

citations.evidence: Myositis-associated interstitial lung disease requires aggressive immunosuppression, particularly if anti-MDA5 positive. Initial treatment: pulse IV methylprednisolone (0.5-1g daily for 3 days) followed by high-dose oral prednisolone. Add cyclophosphamide (IV 0.5-1g/m² monthly) or rituximab (1g IV days 1 and 15) for severe/progressive disease. Monitor closely; mortality high without treatment.
citations.relevance: Provides specific dosing for pulse steroids and additional immunosuppressive agents

question.scenario: A 68-year-old retired ship builder presents with progressive dyspnoea over 2 years. He worked in shipyards for 35 years (1970-2005) and recalls handling asbestos insulation without protective equipment in the 1970s-1980s. He is an ex-smoker (40 pack-years, ceased 15 years ago). Examination reveals bilateral fine late inspiratory crackles at the lung bases and clubbing. High-resolution CT chest shows bilateral subpleural reticular opacities predominantly in the lower lobes, with honeycombing and calcified pleural plaques. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 58% predicted, DLCO 48% predicted, and restrictive pattern. Which of the following statements about his condition is MOST accurate?
question.stem: A 68-year-old retired ship builder presents with progressive dyspnoea over 2 years. He worked in shipyards for 35 years (1970-2005) and recalls handling asbestos insulation without protective equipment in the 1970s-1980s. He is an ex-smoker (40 pack-years, ceased 15 years ago). Examination reveals bilateral fine late inspiratory crackles at the lung bases and clubbing. High-resolution CT chest shows bilateral subpleural reticular opacities predominantly in the lower lobes, with honeycombing and calcified pleural plaques. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 58% predicted, DLCO 48% predicted, and restrictive pattern. Which of the following statements about his condition is MOST accurate?

options.A: The presence of pleural plaques alone is sufficient to diagnose asbestosis without parenchymal changes
options.B: The latency period of 25+ years between exposure and disease onset is typical for asbestosis
options.C: High-dose corticosteroids will significantly improve his lung function and halt disease progression
options.D: His smoking history excludes asbestosis as the cause of interstitial lung disease
options.E: He is not at increased risk of lung cancer as he ceased smoking 15 years ago

mcqs.explanation: Asbestosis is diffuse pulmonary fibrosis caused by inhalation of asbestos fibres. Key features include: (1) Significant asbestos exposure history (occupational exposure in shipbuilding, construction, mining), (2) Long latency period (typically 20-40 years between first exposure and disease onset), (3) Progressive dyspnoea, crackles, clubbing, (4) HRCT showing subpleural reticular opacities, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, predominantly lower lobes, and (5) Restrictive physiology with reduced DLCO. Pleural plaques (calcified or non-calcified pleural thickening) are a marker of asbestos exposure but do NOT cause respiratory symptoms themselves—diagnosis of asbestosis requires parenchymal fibrosis, not just pleural plaques. Latency of 25+ years in this case is typical. Asbestosis has no specific treatment—corticosteroids and immunosuppression are ineffective as fibrosis is non-inflammatory. Management is supportive (oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination, smoking cessation). Asbestos exposure increases risk of: (1) Asbestosis (interstitial fibrosis), (2) Pleural plaques/thickening (benign), (3) Lung cancer (multiplicative risk with smoking—asbestos + smoking increases lung cancer risk 50-90 fold compared to non-smokers without exposure), (4) Mesothelioma (malignant pleural tumour, not related to smoking). Although he ceased smoking 15 years ago, his combined history of asbestos exposure and heavy smoking places him at significantly increased lifetime lung cancer risk. Annual low-dose CT screening may be considered.
mcqs.summary: Australia has high rates of asbestos-related disease due to historical use of asbestos in construction, shipbuilding, and mining (asbestos mining ceased in 1983, imports banned 2003). Asbestosis is a notifiable disease in most Australian states. Workers' compensation available for occupational asbestos disease. Australian Asbestos Network and state-based asbestos diseases support groups provide resources. TSANZ guidelines recommend low-dose CT lung cancer screening for high-risk individuals (asbestos exposure + smoking history).

citations.evidence: Asbestosis is diffuse pulmonary fibrosis from asbestos inhalation. Latency period 20-40 years. HRCT shows subpleural reticular opacities and honeycombing, predominantly lower lobes. Pleural plaques indicate exposure but do not cause symptoms; diagnosis requires parenchymal fibrosis. No specific treatment; management is supportive (oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation). Increased risk of lung cancer (synergistic with smoking) and mesothelioma.
citations.relevance: Establishes diagnostic criteria, typical latency, and lack of specific treatment for asbestosis

citations.source: TSANZ Position Statement on Asbestos-Related Lung Disease (2020)
citations.evidence: Diagnosis of asbestosis requires: (1) confirmed significant asbestos exposure, (2) appropriate latency (usually >20 years), and (3) radiographic evidence of diffuse pulmonary fibrosis (HRCT showing subpleural reticular changes, honeycombing). Pleural plaques alone do not constitute asbestosis. Asbestos exposure + smoking history: consider annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening.
citations.relevance: Confirms pleural plaques alone insufficient for asbestosis diagnosis and screening recommendation

citations.source: Australian Mesothelioma Registry and Australian Asbestos Diseases Society

Asbestos exposure increases lung cancer risk; risk is multiplicative with smoking (50-90 fold increase compared to non-smokers without exposure). Workers' compensation available for occupational asbestos disease in all Australian states. Notifiable disease in most jurisdictions.

question.scenario: A 52-year-old stonemason presents with progressive dyspnoea over 2 years. He has worked in stone benchtop manufacturing for 15 years without regular respiratory protection. High-resolution CT chest shows upper zone predominant nodular opacities with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy demonstrating eggshell calcification. Which investigation is most critical to perform next?
question.stem: A 52-year-old stonemason presents with progressive dyspnoea over 2 years. He has worked in stone benchtop manufacturing for 15 years without regular respiratory protection. High-resolution CT chest shows upper zone predominant nodular opacities with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy demonstrating eggshell calcification. Which investigation is most critical to perform next?

options.A: Serum ACE level to exclude sarcoidosis
options.B: Tuberculosis screening including sputum cultures and QuantiFERON-TB Gold
options.C: Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage for lymphocyte subset analysis
options.D: Pulmonary function tests with DLCO measurement
options.E: Serum precipitins for hypersensitivity pneumonitis

mcqs.explanation: This patient presents with silicosis, an occupational pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of crystalline silica particles. The HRCT findings of upper zone nodules with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes are highly characteristic of silicosis. CRITICAL: Silicosis significantly increases the risk of tuberculosis (TB) reactivation by 2-3 fold due to impaired macrophage function and altered immune responses in silica-exposed lungs. TB screening is MANDATORY in all patients with confirmed or suspected silicosis. This includes: (1) Sputum AFB smear and culture (×3 samples), (2) QuantiFERON-TB Gold or Mantoux test, (3) CXR review for cavitation or infiltrates. Australian occupational health guidelines emphasise early TB detection in silica-exposed workers. While PFTs (D) are important for functional assessment and surveillance, TB screening takes precedence due to the serious public health implications and need for immediate treatment if positive. Serum ACE (A) is less specific, BAL lymphocyte subsets (C) are not diagnostic for silicosis, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis serology (E) is not indicated with clear occupational exposure history and classic imaging.
mcqs.summary: In Australia, silicosis has re-emerged as a major occupational health crisis, particularly in the engineered stone benchtop industry. Safe Work Australia has implemented urgent reforms including mandatory wet cutting, respiratory protection, and health surveillance. The National Dust Disease Taskforce coordinates TB screening protocols for silica-exposed workers. Workers' compensation schemes in NSW, VIC, and QLD provide coverage for silicosis-related conditions including TB.

question.scenario: A 64-year-old former coal miner with 30 years underground work history presents with progressive dyspnoea and cough. CXR shows bilateral upper zone masses (4-6cm) with surrounding nodular opacities. PFTs demonstrate FEV1 45% predicted with reduced DLCO. He has never smoked. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
question.stem: A 64-year-old former coal miner with 30 years underground work history presents with progressive dyspnoea and cough. CXR shows bilateral upper zone masses (4-6cm) with surrounding nodular opacities. PFTs demonstrate FEV1 45% predicted with reduced DLCO. He has never smoked. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

options.A: Simple coal worker's pneumoconiosis with concurrent lung cancer
options.B: Complicated coal worker's pneumoconiosis (progressive massive fibrosis)
options.C: Silicosis with conglomerate masses
options.D: Sarcoidosis with pulmonary fibrosis
options.E: Tuberculosis with post-primary cavitation

mcqs.explanation: This patient has complicated coal worker's pneumoconiosis (CWP), also known as progressive massive fibrosis (PMF). PMF is defined by the presence of large opacities >1cm (typically >3cm) on a background of simple CWP nodules, most commonly in upper zones. PMF develops in 5-15% of miners with simple CWP and represents coalescence of coal dust macules into large fibrotic masses. CLASSIFICATION: Simple CWP shows small rounded nodules 1-10mm without functional impairment. Complicated CWP/PMF shows large masses >1cm with progressive respiratory impairment (reduced FEV1, DLCO) even after cessation of exposure. The bilateral upper zone distribution and 30-year underground mining history with non-smoking status make PMF the most likely diagnosis. Lung cancer (A) would typically present as a solitary mass rather than bilateral symmetric masses. Silicosis (C) has similar imaging but coal mining exposure makes CWP more likely (silicosis requires silica-rich rock like sandstone). Sarcoidosis (D) typically shows lymphadenopathy and responds to steroids. TB (E) would show cavitation with infectious symptoms. MANAGEMENT: No curative treatment exists; supportive care includes supplemental oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, treatment of complications (cor pulmonale, mycobacterial infection). Australian Black Lung screening programs aim for early detection.
mcqs.summary: Coal worker's pneumoconiosis was thought to be eradicated in Australia until re-emergence in Queensland coal miners (2015-present). The Queensland Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis Select Committee led to establishment of the Coal Mine Workers' Health Scheme with mandatory health surveillance including regular CXRs and spirometry. Coal Mine Dust Lung Disease (CMDLD) is a notifiable disease. WorkCover QLD provides compensation and ongoing monitoring for affected miners.

Examination reveals bilateral crackles and SpO2 88% on room air. CXR shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates. WCC 14×10⁹/L with 8% peripheral eosinophils. Bronchoscopy with BAL shows 32% eosinophils. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
question.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to ED with 3-day history of fever (39°C), severe dyspnoea, and dry cough. She started smoking 4 weeks ago. Examination reveals bilateral crackles and SpO2 88% on room air. CXR shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates. WCC 14×10⁹/L with 8% peripheral eosinophils. Bronchoscopy with BAL shows 32% eosinophils. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 days
options.B: Commence empirical antibiotics (ceftriaxone + azithromycin) for severe community-acquired pneumonia
options.C: High-dose oral prednisolone 40-60mg daily with tapering over 2-4 weeks
options.D: Urgent thoracic surgery referral for lung biopsy to confirm diagnosis
options.E: Antifungal therapy with voriconazole for suspected invasive aspergillosis

mcqs.explanation: This patient presents with acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP), a rare acute febrile illness characterised by: (1) Acute onset (<1 month of respiratory symptoms), (2) Hypoxic respiratory failure, (3) Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, (4) BAL eosinophilia >25% (this patient has 32%), (5) Absence of parasitic/fungal infection or drug reaction. KEY TRIGGER: Recent smoking initiation is a well-recognised precipitant of AEP, often seen in military recruits or new smokers. The diagnosis is clinical + BAL eosinophilia without need for biopsy. TREATMENT: Oral prednisolone 40-60mg daily is first-line therapy with rapid response expected within 24-48 hours. Duration 2-4 weeks with tapering. Complete resolution occurs without relapse in most cases. Intravenous methylprednisolone (A) is reserved for life-threatening hypoxaemia requiring mechanical ventilation. Empirical antibiotics (B) may be started initially if bacterial pneumonia cannot be excluded, but should be stopped once AEP is confirmed with BAL. Lung biopsy (D) is not required when BAL shows >25% eosinophils with compatible clinical picture. Antifungals (E) are not indicated without evidence of invasive fungal infection. PROGNOSIS: Excellent with treatment; no recurrence after smoking cessation. Contrast with chronic eosinophilic pneumonia which has peripheral 'photographic negative' pattern and may relapse.
mcqs.summary: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia is rare in Australia but should be considered in acute respiratory failure with recent smoking initiation, military deployment, or new occupational/environmental exposures. BAL is essential for diagnosis and can be performed in tertiary centres with interventional pulmonology services (available in major capital city hospitals). Oral corticosteroids are PBS-subsidised for respiratory indications.

question.scenario: A 58-year-old non-smoker presents with 6-week history of dry cough, dyspnoea, and fatigue. Examination reveals bilateral inspiratory crackles. HRCT chest shows patchy bilateral consolidation with peribronchovascular distribution and areas of ground-glass opacification. A 'reversed halo sign' (central ground-glass with surrounding consolidation ring) is noted in the right lower lobe. Which feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) over other differential diagnoses?
question.stem: A 58-year-old non-smoker presents with 6-week history of dry cough, dyspnoea, and fatigue. Examination reveals bilateral inspiratory crackles. HRCT chest shows patchy bilateral consolidation with peribronchovascular distribution and areas of ground-glass opacification. A 'reversed halo sign' (central ground-glass with surrounding consolidation ring) is noted in the right lower lobe. Which feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) over other differential diagnoses?

options.A: Progressive worsening despite 2 weeks of broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Absence of honeycombing or traction bronchiectasis on HRCT
options.C: Migratory nature of consolidation on serial imaging over 3 weeks
options.D: Presence of peripheral eosinophilia (12% on blood film)
options.E: Elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 85mg/L, ESR 65mm/hr)

mcqs.explanation: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP, formerly BOOP - bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia) is characterised by: (1) Patchy consolidation with peribronchovascular or subpleural distribution, (2) Ground-glass opacification, (3) Reversed halo sign (atoll sign) - central ground-glass surrounded by denser consolidation ring (highly specific for COP), (4) MIGRATORY CONSOLIDATION - lesions resolve in one area while appearing in another ('moving pneumonia'). This migratory pattern (C) is PATHOGNOMONIC and distinguishes COP from bacterial pneumonia or other ILD. The migration reflects the dynamic inflammatory process of organizing pneumonia that 'wanders' through lung parenchyma. Antibiotic failure (A) occurs in many non-infectious conditions and is non-specific. Absence of honeycombing (B) excludes UIP/IPF but doesn't confirm COP (many ILDs lack honeycombing). Peripheral eosinophilia (D) suggests eosinophilic pneumonia rather than COP. Elevated inflammatory markers (E) are non-specific. DIAGNOSIS requires: Clinical + radiological features ± biopsy showing organizing pneumonia pattern (Masson bodies - fibroblast plugs in alveoli). TREATMENT: Prednisolone 0.75-1mg/kg/day (typically 40-60mg) for 4-6 weeks then slow taper over 6-12 months. 60-80% respond dramatically within days. Relapses occur in 30-50% during steroid taper. CAUSES: Idiopathic (cryptogenic) or secondary to infections, drugs, connective tissue disease, radiation.
mcqs.summary: COP diagnosis and management is typically coordinated through specialist respiratory physicians in Australian tertiary centres. HRCT reporting by thoracic radiologists is essential for pattern recognition. Biopsy (surgical or transbronchial cryobiopsy) may be performed if diagnosis uncertain. Prolonged corticosteroid therapy (6-12 months) requires PBS authority prescription for subsidised medication. Monitoring for steroid complications (osteoporosis, diabetes, hypertension) follows RACGP guidelines.

options.B: Pulmonary function tests showing obstructive pattern with reduced DLCO
options.C: Genetic testing for TSC1 or TSC2 mutations
options.D: Transbronchial lung biopsy showing smooth muscle cell proliferation
options.E: Six-minute walk test demonstrating oxygen desaturation

mcqs.explanation: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare cystic lung disease affecting women of childbearing age, characterised by: (1) Diffuse thin-walled cysts on HRCT, (2) Recurrent pneumothorax (most common presentation), (3) Chylous pleural effusions, (4) Progressive airflow obstruction. LAM occurs sporadically or associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). SERUM VEGF-D (vascular endothelial growth factor-D) >800pg/mL has 70% sensitivity and 95% specificity for LAM diagnosis, making it the BEST non-invasive diagnostic test. VEGF-D reflects lymphatic involvement and correlates with disease severity. DIAGNOSTIC ALGORITHM: Premenopausal woman + characteristic HRCT cysts + VEGF-D >800pg/mL = LAM diagnosis confirmed without biopsy. If VEGF-D <800pg/mL or diagnostic uncertainty, lung biopsy (surgical or transbronchial cryobiopsy) is required showing smooth muscle cell proliferation positive for HMB-45. PFTs (B) show obstructive pattern but are not specific. TSC genetic testing (C) identifies associated cases but only 30-40% of LAM patients have TSC. Transbronchial biopsy (D) has low yield due to patchy distribution; surgical biopsy preferred if needed. 6MWT (E) assesses functional capacity but doesn't confirm diagnosis. MANAGEMENT: mTOR inhibitor sirolimus slows FEV1 decline (MILES trial). Lung transplantation for end-stage disease.
mcqs.summary: LAM is ultra-rare in Australia (prevalence ~1-2 per million women). Diagnosis and management are centralised through specialist ILD clinics in major tertiary centres (e.g., Royal Prince Alfred Hospital Sydney, Alfred Hospital Melbourne). Serum VEGF-D testing is available through specialist pathology labs. Sirolimus therapy requires specialist respiratory physician prescription and is available through Special Access Scheme (not PBS-listed for LAM). LAM Australasia patient support network coordinates care and research participation.

question.scenario: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnoea over 12 months. He is a non-smoker who works as a sandblaster. HRCT shows bilateral ground-glass opacification with superimposed interlobular septal thickening creating a 'crazy-paving' pattern. BAL reveals milky fluid with PAS-positive proteinaceous material. Serum GM-CSF autoantibodies are positive. What is the definitive treatment for this condition?
question.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnoea over 12 months. He is a non-smoker who works as a sandblaster. HRCT shows bilateral ground-glass opacification with superimposed interlobular septal thickening creating a 'crazy-paving' pattern. BAL reveals milky fluid with PAS-positive proteinaceous material. Serum GM-CSF autoantibodies are positive. What is the definitive treatment for this condition?

options.A: High-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 1mg/kg daily) for immunosuppression
options.B: Whole lung lavage under general anaesthesia with sequential single-lung ventilation
options.C: Inhaled GM-CSF (sargramostim) to restore surfactant clearance
options.D: Rituximab infusion to deplete GM-CSF autoantibody-producing B cells
options.E: Cessation of silica exposure and supportive oxygen therapy only

mcqs.explanation: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) is a rare disease characterised by accumulation of surfactant-like lipoproteinaceous material in alveoli due to impaired macrophage clearance. TYPES: (1) Autoimmune PAP (90%) - anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies impair macrophage function, (2) Secondary PAP - silica exposure, haematological malignancy, immunosuppression, (3) Congenital PAP - genetic surfactant mutations. IMAGING: 'Crazy-paving' pattern on HRCT (ground-glass + interlobular septal thickening) is highly characteristic. DIAGNOSIS: BAL milky fluid with PAS-positive material + serum GM-CSF autoantibodies confirms autoimmune PAP. TREATMENT: Whole lung lavage (WLL) is the DEFINITIVE therapy, performed under general anaesthesia with double-lumen endotracheal tube allowing sequential single-lung ventilation. One lung is lavaged with 1-2L aliquots of warmed normal saline (total 10-40L) while the other lung is ventilated. Procedure repeated for opposite lung 1-2 weeks later. WLL physically removes accumulated surfactant, providing symptomatic improvement for months to years. 80-90% response rate. Corticosteroids (A) are INEFFECTIVE in PAP. Inhaled GM-CSF (C) has shown benefit in small studies but is not first-line (used for refractory cases). Rituximab (D) is experimental for reducing autoantibody levels. Exposure cessation (E) is important for secondary PAP but doesn't treat established disease. This patient likely has secondary PAP from silica exposure (sandblasting) but still requires WLL.
mcqs.summary: Whole lung lavage for PAP is performed at specialised centres in Australia (RPA Sydney, Alfred Melbourne, Royal Brisbane Hospital) by interventional pulmonologists and thoracic anaesthetists. The procedure requires ICU/HDU monitoring post-operatively. GM-CSF autoantibody testing is available through specialist immunology labs. Inhaled GM-CSF (sargramostim) is not TGA-approved and requires Special Access Scheme application. Occupational PAP cases (silica exposure) are notifiable and compensable under workers' compensation schemes.
